overview.headline: CoRL 2026 tripled in size and largely converged on its ingredients (large pretrained policies, human video, world models, frontier-model planners) while openly disputing whether that recipe produces robots anyone will pay for.
summary: The tenth CoRL drew 2,094 submissions, about three times the roughly 700 of 2025, and around 4,800 attendees across three Austin venues. Program chairs kept the 32.8% acceptance rate and a single track by adding a poster-only tier and 3-minute spotlights. The top submission keywords were manipulation, imitation learning, perception/control representations, RL and robot foundation models, and the accepted papers followed that distribution closely. A new late-breaking track on agentic robotics and real-to-sim-to-real responded to frontier models released only months before.

On stage, the technical picture was more settled than the strategic one. Physical Intelligence, NVIDIA, Google DeepMind and many academic labs presented the same stack: a large BC-pretrained policy, human egocentric data for scale, world models for data and evaluation, and a frontier model on top for planning. The disagreement was about whether this stack reaches reliable, profitable deployment. Polls before and after the closing debate on that question leaned against the motion and barely moved. Ken Goldberg described the field as being in a 'revenue crisis', meaning it now has to deliver reliability, throughput and interpretability.

themes.title: Frontier models on top, fast policies underneath
themes.body: Most systems put a slow reasoner over a fast learned controller. Hang Zhao reported that frontier models used as step-by-step policies under a real clock fell to 15-20% success on RoboCasa, and argued that most failures happen at the handoffs between layers. Boston Dynamics said no off-the-shelf VLM was reliable enough to check task completion without fine-tuning. In the debate, Vanhoucke said general-purpose models were beating the conference's robot models on some robotics benchmarks; Agrawal answered that contact-rich System 1 data is still missing from those models.

themes.title: World models used as policies, simulators and evaluators
themes.body: DreamZero and GR00T 2 jointly denoise video and actions. DreamZero's authors found that failures originate mostly in video generation, so better video backbones should mean better actions. SuperMimic won Best Paper by training a humanoid tracker through one learned differentiable dynamics model in about three GPU-hours. Tesla warned that training inside a world model, rather than only evaluating with one, lets policies exploit its physical errors. Another spotlight showed world models can be poisoned.

themes.title: Human data is the main source of scale, but it needs a bridge
themes.body: EgoScale showed human-data validation loss following a log-linear scaling law that tracks real-robot success. It also found that the hardest dexterous tasks needed an aligned mid-training stage (about 4 hours of teleop paired with 50 hours of matched human data). Ego2Robot found hand-pose accuracy limits its gains on precise tasks.

themes.title: Force and touch are being added to VLAs
themes.body: Several papers traced VLA failures in contact-rich tasks to missing force signals or to flow-matching noise schedules that underweight small near-contact actions. The fixes are cheap: learned torque estimates for commodity arms, tactile arrows drawn on images, and force experts added late in post-training. Burgard and Sharpa both argued that robot foundation models need force and touch.

themes.title: RL returns as targeted post-training
themes.body: RL was mostly applied on top of a pretrained generalist, not as a replacement for one. RL Token runs a small actor-critic on compressed VLA embeddings to fix a task's hardest step within hours; its Ethernet-insertion episodes were faster than an expert teleoperator's. π0.7 instead conditions on quality metadata so it can learn from mixed-quality data, and Play2Perfect shows that RL play pretraining in simulation makes sparse-reward assembly learnable.

themes.title: Evaluation is not trusted
themes.body: A best-paper finalist showed that a DINO-plus-MLP policy nearly matches the best reported LIBERO scores, and that few reported gains are statistically significant. RoboColosseum estimated 400-500 comparisons are needed per significant conclusion. LIBERO-CF found VLAs often ignore language when they see objects from training tasks.

themes.title: Deployment numbers and the revenue question
themes.body: Industry talks reported operating metrics. Atlas sequencing parts at Hyundai: 98.6% completion with a 9.5% intervention rate, but cycle time is about 50% too slow to pay off. Walden's Toyota camshaft cell has never stopped the line. Gemini Robotics 2.5 reported 96% autonomous kitting. The debate split on whether paying people to collect in-domain data can ever be economical outside tasks like laundry.

since_2025.title: Three times the papers, twice the people
since_2025.body: Seoul accepted 263 papers, from roughly 700 submissions according to the 2026 chairs, and an unofficial count put in-person attendance at 2,441. Austin received 2,094 submissions and had about 4,800 attendees, and to handle them it added a poster-only tier, senior area chairs, a first-round rejection before rebuttal, and citation screening.

since_2025.title: Awards moved from task results to learning machinery
since_2025.body: In 2025 the Best Paper awards went to unified position/force control for legged loco-manipulation and to Fabrica's dual-arm assembly, and π0.5 and DexUMI were finalists. The 2026 winners were a learned world model used to train humanoid control (SuperMimic) and context scaling (RoboTTT).

since_2025.title: Model releases are now measured in factories
since_2025.body: Google DeepMind announced Gemini Robotics 1.5 around CoRL 2025. In Austin, Gemini Robotics 2.5 came with a production-line kitting pilot. Physical Intelligence went from π0.5 to π0.7. The 2025 special panel discussed humanoid learning; the 2026 one debated commercial viability.

since_2025.title: From VLAs and real2sim to agents and world models
since_2025.body: A 2025 survey named VLAs, Real2Sim2Real and tactile sensing as CoRL's main themes. All three continued in 2026, and Real2Sim2Real got its own late-breaking track. What is new is the agentic robotics track and world action models trained jointly on video and actions, which were not 2025 themes.

outlook_2027.title: Evaluation norms will tighten in Paris
outlook_2027.body: Prediction: more papers will report confidence intervals and use held-out or post-release test sets, and reviewers will question gains on LIBERO and SimplerEnv. Evidence: a best-paper finalist on exactly this, RoboColosseum's free evaluation offer, and keynote calls for deadline and interventions-per-hour metrics.

outlook_2027.title: Layer interfaces become the research object
outlook_2027.body: Prediction: work will shift to what passes between System 1 and System 2: failure signals going up, force or contact intent going down. Evidence: Zhao's handoff-failure analysis, Agrawal's claim that System 1 is the bottleneck, and agentic harnesses at NVIDIA and Boston Dynamics.

outlook_2027.title: World models will be judged on whether you can train in them
outlook_2027.body: Prediction: world-model papers will need to show that policies trained inside them don't exploit errors, and that success predicted inside the model matches real-world success, not just that the video looks right. Evidence: Tesla's warning, MemWorld's still-underestimated success, and the poisoning attack.

outlook_2027.title: Throughput replaces success rate in deployment claims
outlook_2027.body: Prediction: 2027 industry talks will lead with cycle time, mean time between interventions and number of robots per remote operator. Boston Dynamics forecast Atlas's first 8-hour shift in 2027, and Goldberg framed the year's challenge as revenue. Whether BC pretraining plus in-domain data clears that bar will remain contested.

takeaways: The field has largely converged on a stack; the open question is economics, not architecture.
Frontier models help as planners but failed as direct step-by-step controllers under a real clock.
Human egocentric data scales, but precise dexterity still needed aligned robot-and-human mid-training.
Force and touch can be added to existing VLAs cheaply, and doing so fixes specific contact failures.
Most RL now targets a pretrained generalist's bottleneck step instead of training from scratch.
Popular simulation benchmarks can be largely solved by memorization, and most reported gains are within noise.
Best Paper went to training humanoid control inside a learned differentiable world model.
Deployments reach about 99% completion with interventions but remain too slow to pay off.

talks.title: Welcome and Opening Remarks
talks.summary: General chair Yuke Zhu opens the tenth CoRL, noting that attendance doubled and submissions roughly tripled to nearly 2,100 papers, and explains the South by Southwest-style format spread across the Hilton, JW Marriott and UT's Bass Concert Hall. The program chairs describe the new three-tier program (orals, 3-minute spotlights, poster-only), a 32.8% acceptance rate, the new late-breaking results track on agentic robotics and real-to-sim-to-real, senior area chairs, and a policy that desk-rejected about a dozen papers for hallucinated citations. Workshop, demo, local and inclusion chairs then cover half-day workshops, 17 demos, venues, lunch, Wi-Fi, travel awards and child care, and Peter Stone closes with an overview of Texas Robotics and the new UT School of Computing before thanking the sponsors.
takeaways: Submissions rose from about 700 to nearly 2,100, forcing a three-tier presentation format to keep the conference single track.
The acceptance rate stayed near past years at 32.8%, and the accepted papers' keyword distribution closely matched that of all submissions.
For the first time, papers with multiple hallucinated or incorrect citations were flagged and about a dozen were desk rejected, while other AI-assisted writing was left to author judgment.
A first-round rejection removed a little over a third of submissions before rebuttal, so that review effort focused on papers with at least one champion.
Student registration was cut to $200, below cost, and subsidized by sponsors to lower barriers for students.
Workshops were made half-day to encourage interactive discussion over mini-conference talk lineups, with 32 of 78 valid proposals accepted.

talks.title: MolmoAct2: Action Reasoning Models for Real-World Deployment
talks.affiliation: Allen Institute for AI / University of Washington / National University of Singapore
talks.summary: The authors present MolmoAct2, a fully open robotics foundation model with an open recipe covering pre-training, mid-training and adaptation, connecting a spatially specialized VLM to an action expert and reasoning adaptively about depth instead of regenerating it every step. It outperforms strong baselines out of the box on open embodied-reasoning benchmarks and was also evaluated blind by a third-party company after fine-tuning.
takeaways: Depth reasoning is updated adaptively rather than regenerating every token at each time step, keeping reasoning-augmented control efficient.
Blind third-party evaluation was used for the first time to assess the fine-tuned model.
The authors argue openness pays off: the MolmoAct models and data have been downloaded more than 1.5 million times on Hugging Face, which helps them learn what transfers.

talks.title: Semantic Anchoring for Robotic Action Representations
talks.summary: Inspired by mirror neurons, the authors show that VLA action representations lose their alignment with pretrained vision-language semantics during fine-tuning, and that this alignment correlates with task success. They split features into a shared semantic path aligned with a frozen VLM and a private path that keeps execution details, improving several VLAs (including pi0) in simulation and on real robots.
takeaways: Semantic alignment of action representations measurably erodes during fine-tuning and tracks both rollout success and out-of-distribution generalization.
Aligning all features to semantics hurts execution, so a shared/private feature split is needed to preserve physical details.
Gains are larger on generalization axes such as compositional tasks than on in-domain tasks.

talks.title: MEM: Multi-Scale Embodied Memory for Vision Language Action Models
talks.summary: The authors add multi-scale memory to VLAs: short-term visual memory of the last few seconds compressed by a video encoder and fed to the low-level policy, plus long-term textual memory in which the VLM recurrently predicts a summary of past events. This lets policies handle tasks lasting up to 15 minutes, such as preparing a recipe and cleaning the kitchen.
takeaways: Naively feeding raw video history is infeasible: one hour at 50 Hz with 256 tokens per image is about 50 million tokens.
Ablations show both long-term text memory and short-term video memory are needed to solve the long-horizon tasks.
Memory enables in-context adaptation, where the policy notices a failed attempt and tries a different strategy instead of repeating the same mistake.

talks.title: PRTS: A Primitive Reasoning and Tasking System via Contrastive Representations
talks.summary: PRTS reformulates VLA pretraining as goal-conditioned contrastive RL, treating language instructions as goals so that state-action embeddings capture progress toward the goal without reward annotation, combined with action-token prediction and scaled to 400 million samples. The resulting policy recovers from heavy human interference, follows novel instructions zero-shot and handles unseen situations in long-horizon tray clearing.
takeaways: Same-instruction steps are treated as positives and later steps are weighted more, so the embedding encodes temporal progress toward the goal.
The contrastive pretraining needs no extra reward labels, and downstream post-training uses standard behavior cloning with a fresh flow-matching action expert.
The policy handled an empty-bowl case absent from all demonstrations, suggesting progress-aware representations aid recovery.
author_affiliations: TeleAI, China Telecom / Shanghai Jiao Tong University

talks.title: Learning What to Say to Your VLA: Mostly Harmless Vision Language Action Model Steering
talks.summary: The authors learn a language feedback policy that steers a frozen VLA by searching locally perturbed language sequences, rolling them out closed loop, and distilling the best ones into a VLM via rejection fine-tuning. An improvement head with conformal prediction decides when to intervene, giving a do-no-harm guarantee, and success rises on pi0.5 and MolmoAct2 in simulation and on hardware.
takeaways: VLA language-to-action mappings are brittle, so rephrasing an instruction can change behavior unpredictably.
Conformal prediction on the improvement head lets the system fall back to the original instruction when steering is unlikely to help.
Steering through language alone improves VLA performance without updating the underlying policy weights.

talks.title: When Vision Overrides Language: Evaluating and Mitigating Counterfactual Failures in VLAs
talks.affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
talks.summary: The authors introduce LIBERO-CF, a benchmark of over 50 counterfactual tasks showing that VLAs often ignore language and repeat well-learned training tasks because of vision shortcuts. They propose Counterfactual Action Guidance, a dual-branch inference scheme that amplifies the difference between language-conditioned and unconditioned action predictions, improving language grounding in simulation and with pi0.5 on real robots.
takeaways: VLAs on LIBERO reach high success even with vision-only input, revealing strong reliance on visual cues.
Counterfactual failures are triggered by the presence of training-task objects; removing them helps the policy follow the instruction.
CAG needs no extra demonstrations or changes to the base VLA architecture or weights.

talks.title: ZETA: A Controlled Study of Zero-Shot Cross-Embodiment VLA Transfer for Tabletop Manipulation
talks.summary: The authors separate strict zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer from pretrain-exposed transfer and build a controlled benchmark with 14 unseen target robots in simulation and the real world, where only the robot changes. They study representation, source diversity, auxiliary objectives and target exposure.
takeaways: Representing states and actions as deltas in the gripper's own frame raised average progress from 60 to 76 in simulation and from 56 to 90 on real robots.
More source robots help by about 18 points, but only if each robot still receives enough data under a fixed budget.
Replacing just 5% of training data with target-robot data lifted the Google robot from 51 to 69, so strict and pretrain-exposed results should be reported separately.

talks.title: EmbodiSteer: Steering Embodiment-Agnostic Visuomotor Policies with Joint-Space Guidance for Zero-Shot Cross-Embodiment Deployment
talks.summary: EmbodiSteer keeps a Cartesian visuomotor policy, trained from handheld-gripper data, frozen and moves diffusion sampling into the target robot's joint space via forward kinematics and the Jacobian. An optimization-based guidance at each denoising step balances collision clearance against changes to end-effector motion, enabling zero-shot, body-aware deployment across nine simulated and two real robots.
takeaways: Denoising in joint space leaves task performance almost unchanged while adding whole-body awareness.
Naive gradient-based collision guidance pulls the gripper off the task, so the constraint must be balanced against end-effector motion.
On real tasks, success nearly doubled and collisions fell from 97% to 7% without robot-specific training.

talks.title: Diagnosing Compositional Generalization in Sequential Robot Tasks
talks.summary: The authors decompose the compositional generalization gap in sequential tasks into marginal instruction shift, instruction-compositional shift and context-action shift, and use it to ask which instruction combinations a robot actually needs to see. Experiments show sparse but well-chosen coverage suffices, and that failures under sparse coverage stem from instruction steering rather than missing skills.
takeaways: Full combinatorial coverage is unnecessary; a carefully chosen quarter of the data can match full training.
Adding a single demonstration per task fixes many sparse-coverage failures, pointing to instruction steering as the bottleneck.
When instructions depend on each other, relational coverage of dependent pairs is required and modular policies with oracle high-level indicators fail.

talks.title: Organizing Physical AI Across Timescales
talks.summary: Introduced by Chen Feng, Hang Zhao argues that robot intelligence should be split by timescale rather than function: S2 reasoning over seconds, S1 policies at tens of hertz and S0 control at hundreds of hertz. In a RoboCasa study with a real clock, frontier models used as direct or agentic step-by-step policies collapsed to 15-20% success, while orchestrated designs that pair a slow model with fast learned skills held up. He draws on lessons from DriveVLM's dual system in production cars and from robot parkour, then presents three ways to keep S1 fast: FastWAM, which learns from video at training time but skips video generation at test time (G0-7); turning off chain-of-thought at inference in G0.5; and the streaming action tokenizer ActionCodec 2. He closes by arguing that interfaces between layers need richer feedback going up and force or contact intent going down, and he asks benchmarks to report success under a deadline along with inference time.
takeaways: Slow frontier models are fine when combined with a fast lower layer, but used as step-by-step direct policies under a real clock they fail most tasks.
Layer boundaries should be drawn where the required reaction time changes: task and scene at seconds, hand-object motion at tens of hertz, contact and force at hundreds of hertz.
Skipping chain-of-thought at inference made no difference on about 90% of tasks and doubled speed, helping mainly on long multi-stage tasks.
Skipping future-video generation at test time sped up a world action model by more than four times, and the 16B G0-7 runs at 60 ms per action on an RTX 5090.
Most failures occur at handoffs between layers, because lower layers cannot report failure upward and motion-only commands omit force.
Zhao suggests S2 belongs in the cloud, S1 on edge servers shared by multiple robots, and S0 on the robot itself.

talks.title: π0.7: a Steerable Generalist Robotic Foundation Model with Emergent Capabilities
talks.summary: Physical Intelligence presents π0.7, a generalist robot foundation model trained with rich multimodal prompts: subgoal images, detailed subtask instructions, and metadata describing how a task was performed (e.g., quality, mistakes, speed). Out of the box, a single model matches or sometimes exceeds the task-specific RL-post-trained π*0.6 on laundry folding, espresso making and box folding, and also performs tasks from earlier PI releases without fine-tuning. Metadata lets the model learn from mixed-quality teleoperation and evaluation data, and the authors highlight emergent compositional generalization such as folding shirts on a UR5 bimanual setup with no UR5 laundry data. In Q&A they explain that quality labels come largely from post-hoc human annotation, with speed as one signal that correlates well with quality.
takeaways: Without metadata prompts, adding progressively lower-quality laundry data made performance drop, while with metadata performance kept improving as data grew.
Conditioning on quality metadata lets the model separate good from bad behaviors so high-quality behavior can simply be requested at test time, similar to telling an LLM to act as an expert.
π0.7 transferred laundry folding to a UR5 bimanual industrial arm despite large embodiment differences from the lightweight arms used for data collection.
Determining data quality remains an open, iterative problem; PI relies on post-hoc annotations refined by what correlates with real-world performance.

talks.title: Being-H0.5: Scaling Human-Centric Robot Learning for Cross-Embodiment Generalization
talks.summary: The authors present Being-H0.5, a VLA that uses human hand interaction data as a universal anchor across robot embodiments, addressing the scarcity and imbalance of robot data from about 30 embodiments. Its corpus combines reconstructed hand motion from egocentric human video, about 14,000 hours of robot data and about 5,000 hours of vision-language data, trained in a shared slot-based action space with motion generation, description and continuation tasks. Robot-specific specialization uses a mixture-of-flow action expert, a manifold-preserving gating mechanism for observation shift, and universal async chunking that extends RTC with per-robot delays. A single generalist checkpoint across five embodiments stays close to per-robot specialists and does better on generalization.
takeaways: Human-centric pretraining narrowed the generalist-vs-specialist gap, which grew substantially when training from scratch.
A task collected only on a Unitree G1 transferred to a different robot at a non-zero success rate with pretraining, while the scratch model failed completely.
Treating the human hand as just another embodiment in a shared action-slot space lets human wrist motion supervise robot end-effector slots with the same loss.
Hand-motion labels mostly come from reconstruction pipelines filtered by heuristic quality metrics, supplemented by open-source datasets with hand labels.

talks.title: RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies
talks.summary: RoboTTT scales a robot policy's visuomotor context to 8,000 timesteps by inserting test-time-training (TTT) layers, whose fast weights are updated by gradient descent at both training and inference, across per-timestep outputs of GR00T N1.7's DiT action blocks. Training uses sequence action forcing (independent noise levels per action chunk) and loss masks that separate context from imitation targets, enabling in-context imitation from human videos and DAgger distillation where the model learns to correct its own failures. On long-horizon assembly tasks it reaches 79% average task completion at constant inference latency, and is the only method to complete all ten stages of a gear-bot assembly. The model was also mid-trained on long-horizon human video (EgoScale).
takeaways: Closed-loop performance rose steadily with context length, 63% better at 8K than at 1K context, while a gated DeltaNet alternative did not scale.
Fast weights act as a fixed-size recurrent state, giving constant memory and latency regardless of context length.
Sampling noise levels independently per action chunk stabilizes sequence training on temporally correlated robot trajectories.
Placing a human hand demonstration in context let the robot perform unseen assembly configurations one-shot.

talks.title: World Action Models are Zero-shot Policies
talks.summary: The authors introduce DreamZero, a 14B autoregressive World Action Model built from a pretrained video diffusion model and fine-tuned to jointly denoise future video frames and actions with a teacher-forcing objective. Chunk-wise autoregressive denoising enables KV caching and lets the model condition on real observations during execution, and system and model optimizations cut per-chunk inference from 5.7 s to 0.15 s (a 38x speedup on GB200). On AgiBot and DROID-Franka setups it outperforms VLA baselines, including cross-embodiment-pretrained ones, on seen and unseen tasks, and keeps its advantage after task-specific post-training.
takeaways: Training on diverse, non-repetitive data across environments and tasks lets the model inherit the video model's zero-shot generalization.
Making a video model fast enough for real-time control was the main engineering challenge.
The authors observed that video and action predictions stay well aligned, and that failures mostly originate in video generation, so better video backbones should yield better actions.
Failure data was not used in pretraining; using it for test-time adaptation is left to future work.

talks.title: Memory-augmented Action-conditioned World Model for Robot Manipulation
talks.summary: MemWorld addresses action-conditioned world models that distort objects when they leave and re-enter the wrist camera view during long rollouts. Its surfel-based memory links scene surfaces to the times they were observed; future camera poses computed from the upcoming action chunk are used to render and score surfels for visibility, task relevance and recency, retrieving the top-K historical frames as context for a multi-view world model. On 34 challenging DROID trajectories it improves visual consistency over Ctrl-World, it tracks real policy performance more closely, and its imagined rollouts can be used to fine-tune policies. The talk was delivered by a non-author because the authors could not travel, and Q&A was skipped.
takeaways: Future robot actions are a direct cue for which past observations to retrieve, because they determine where the wrist camera will look next.
Correlation between world-model and real-world success for π0 and π0.5 on five tasks improved from 0.85 to 0.97, though success is still underestimated.
Fine-tuning π0.5 on 20–30 selected successful imagined rollouts per task raised average real-world success on three long-horizon tasks from 58% to 72%.
Multi-view consistency and explicit physical constraints remain open challenges.
author_affiliations: Dalian University of Technology / Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing

talks.title: TEMPO: Learning Temporal Context for Dynamic Robot Manipulation
talks.summary: TEMPO targets dynamic manipulation tasks (bottle handover from a walking person, drop catch, flick catch and pouring into a moving basket) where single-frame VLAs fail even with latency-reduction methods like RTC. It adds two missing ingredients: motion tokens from temporal attention over a frozen video foundation model's features of recent frames (SAM 2 by default, about 11 ms per frame), and a compact proprioceptive history of recent joint commands fed to both the VLM and the action expert. The history resolves cases where visually similar states call for opposite actions. Everything runs on academic-scale compute, and the code and data are open-sourced.
takeaways: Cutting inference latency alone does not solve dynamic tasks; policies also need object velocity and their own action history.
On bottle handover, TEMPO halved complete misses and nearly doubled successes relative to the base VLA, which missed entirely in 18 of 50 episodes.
Each ingredient alone beats the base VLA, together they reach 74%, and the gains held across three different VLA backbones.
Motion understanding is capped by the video foundation model's pretraining, so very fast motions such as thrown balls can still fail.

talks.title: Diversity You Can Actually Measure: A Fast, Model-Free Diversity Metric for Robotics Datasets
talks.summary: The authors propose signature entropy, a non-parametric diversity measure for robot demonstration datasets: each demonstration is treated as a path over flattened states, actions and (embedded) observations, mapped through the signature transform, and compared with the signature kernel. Entropy is computed in closed form from the kernel matrix's eigenvalues, with a determinant-based volumetric alternative. They also introduce FACTUAL, a model-free curation algorithm that greedily selects the subset maximizing entropy. On RoboMimic, FACTUAL beats random pruning and sometimes the full dataset, and a similar trend holds with a small VLA on a real robot.
takeaways: Signature entropy correlated strongly with policy success on RoboMimic, with Pearson coefficients from 0.74 to 1 across architectures from RNNs to diffusion policies.
The signature transform handles trajectories of different lengths while preserving path geometry, avoiding the need for an intractable probability distribution.
FACTUAL needs no auxiliary model, policy access or rollouts, making it far lighter than other curation methods.
Dataset entropy saturates as demonstrations are added, and the saturation rate reflects how diverse the underlying data is.
author_affiliations: University of Toronto / Allen Institute for AI

talks.title: MolmoB0T: Large-Scale Simulation Enables Zero-Shot Manipulation
talks.summary: MolmoBot is a family of manipulation policies trained only on simulated data that transfer zero-shot to real robots. The MolmoBot engine builds on the MolmoSpaces asset ecosystem to sample scenes, objects and receptacles, aggressively randomize robot joints, lighting, textures and cameras, and generate demonstrations from a scripted state machine with retries and action noise. The result is MolmoBot data with 1.7 million demonstrations across about 94,000 environments. Policies (MolmoBot based on Molmo 2, a lightweight MolmoBot-SPOC, and MolmoBot-Pi0) were tested with 120 real trials per policy on a Franka DROID setup and on an RB-Y1 mobile manipulator, and everything is open-sourced.
takeaways: MolmoBot-Pi0 shares π0's architecture but is trained only on synthetic data, and it still performs strongly in the real world, showing that sim data alone can train robust VLAs.

The authors' practical rule is that anything that can be randomized should be randomized; aggressive camera randomization made the policies robust to large camera motion without ignoring the exo camera.
Ablations show data scale consistently helps while object-class and environment diversity saturate past a threshold on simple pick tasks.
Deformables are not yet supported, but MuJoCo's new native deformable support opens that direction.

talks.title: What Are We Actually Benchmarking in Robot Manipulation?
talks.summary: The authors examine five widely reported manipulation benchmarks and identify four ways a high score can mislead: shortcuts, gains within noise, fragility to small in-distribution shifts, and data advantages mistaken for generalization. A simple DINO-plus-MLP policy with no robot pretraining or language understanding nearly matches the best reported LIBERO results because reset distributions barely vary, and few reported gains on SimplerEnv and LIBERO are statistically significant. Sampling test poses from the wider training range lowers every policy's score, and a tiny policy trained on scripted in-simulation demos nears the best SimplerEnv scores. They attribute most problems to public, fixed, narrow test sets and propose post-release or extremely diverse test sets plus explicit confidence-interval guidance.
takeaways: Benchmarks such as LIBERO and CALVIN can be solved largely by memorizing where to act, since test initial states are nearly covered by training demos.
Papers rarely report standard deviations or per-rollout outcomes, so small improvements often cannot be distinguished from chance.
Since evaluation protocols do not restrict training data sources, a SimplerEnv score alone cannot show real-to-sim generalization.
Any public, fixed benchmark will be overfit, increasingly so now that LLM agents can iterate against it, so hidden or very diverse test sets are needed.

talks.title: Scaling Robotic Dexterity Toward Real-World Applications
talks.summary: Lu frames dexterous manipulation as the last unsolved piece of general-purpose robots, bottlenecked by data that must capture contacts, forces and recovery. He describes three complementary paths at Sharpa: expanding data sources through hardware-software co-design (the W2 tactile hand, D01 robot and AE01 exoskeleton glove, shared-autonomy teleoperation and human-centric visuo-tactile capture), a fast tactile 'System 0' interaction layer beneath System 1/2 policies, and cross-embodiment tactile learning via a morphology-aware token space. He closes with the company timeline and a fully autonomous robotic ice cream store deployment.
takeaways: Teleoperation data is slow and costly while video lacks contact and force, so Sharpa combines human-centric glove capture with robot data rather than replacing one with the other.
A low-level interaction layer that uses sensing close to the contact point is positioned as the place where high-quality tactile sensing matters most ('the last millimeter').
Mapping heterogeneous tactile sensors into a shared morphology-aware token space lets one tactile expert transfer experience across sensors and embodiments.
A real store deployment making a 55-step ice cream order end to end is used as a comprehensive reliability test of the full stack.

talks.title: Scaling Robot Learning Through Data and Simulation
talks.summary: Ureno presents Lightwheel's loop of egocentric human data, physics-validated simulation and evaluation for training robot policies. He covers EgoSuite egocentric datasets (an open 10k-hour release scaling toward 100k), the SimFoundry real-to-sim pipeline with a measurement factory for calibrating friction, damping and deformable objects such as cables, and RoboFinals as an evaluation benchmark plus new RL environments built from real industrial tasks. In Q&A he explains that measured real-world oscillation data is used to reverse-engineer simulator parameters.
takeaways: Training a policy is framed as needing three things: useful examples, a place to practice, and a way to measure.
Deformable assets such as cables are calibrated by matching simulated and real oscillation-and-settling curves to close the real-to-sim gap.
Lightwheel argues that RL environments built from real industrial tasks are more valuable than tabletop teleoperation tasks.
Environment construction is done agentically with simulation engineers reviewing each step for physical fidelity.

talks.title: From Dreaming to Doing: World Action Models and Agentic Robotics
talks.summary: Fan argues that the arrival of a powerful frontier model ('Astra') does not make a fast System 1 obsolete, and that the real question is what makes a good, teachable and steerable skill. He presents GR00T 2, a 2B-parameter world action model that jointly predicts future video frames and actions in one diffusion pass, plus a Turbo variant for edge compute, demonstrated on long-horizon dexterous tasks like data-center memory swaps and chemistry-lab procedures. He shows 'cross adapt' zero-shot transfer from human wearables, mocap gloves, DexUMI exoskeletons and simulation, and three ways to couple the frontier model with GR00T (visual steering, action edits, and the Aspire agentic harness). He closes by announcing open releases of model weights, SimFoundry, Aspire, the Flora annotation suite, 100k hours of human data and hardware designs.
takeaways: The model 'dreams' future frames in pixel space and acts on them, decoding action and video jointly.
Fine-tuning only on human-collected data (UMI grippers, mocap gloves, DexUMI exoskeletons) transferred zero-shot to different robot hardware.
Painting guidance onto pixels lets a large reasoning model steer a small policy, offloading cognition such as Tower of Hanoi recursion upstream.
An agentic harness that switches between the learned policy and code-as-policy recovery skills enabled near-continuous assembly through the night.
NVIDIA announced GR00T 2 and Turbo weights plus the cross-adapt recipe would be open-sourced in December.

talks.title: How Can Robots Learn to Interact and Coordinate with Others?
talks.summary: Mehr, introduced by Ken Goldberg, uses a two-robot cooperative carrying task to show why learning interaction differs from single-agent learning. For imitation, she explains that multi-agent behavior cloning must care about exploitability rather than value gap, uses decentralized diffusion policies to handle multimodal coordination, and learns residual denoisers that add coordination on top of frozen single-agent policies. For RL, she shows foundation models acting as 'coaches' that decompose tasks, write reward and composition code, and perform credit assignment, enabling tasks that plain MAPPO could not solve. Finally, she casts continual learning as temporal consensus in weight space, solved with primal-dual method-of-multipliers updates, which fine-tunes pi-0.5 on new tasks without forgetting pre-training tasks and without replay.
takeaways: In multi-agent imitation, a small deviation by one agent can doom the joint task, so data coverage of failure and interaction modes matters even more than in single-agent settings.
Decentralized diffusion policies run in receding horizon can implicitly agree on one coordination mode without communication.
Freezing pretrained single-agent policies and learning only a coordination residual from few demonstrations retains solo skills while enabling teamwork.
Using an off-the-shelf foundation model as a credit assigner outperformed standard multi-agent RL baselines in a warehouse coordination task.
Iterating on coach-generated skill-composition code raised a humanoid button-pushing success rate from about 20% to 90% in two rounds.
Replay-free temporal consensus (TACO) retained pre-training task performance where supervised fine-tuning forgot it, and also avoided duplicate or stale objects in dynamic mapping.

talks.title: BitVLA: 1-bit Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotics Manipulation
talks.affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences / University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
talks.summary: The authors present BitVLA, a fully native 1-bit VLA with ternary weights built on BitNet b1.58, using a Quantize-then-Distill stage to compress the vision encoder. It matches OpenVLA-OFT-level manipulation while using 11x less memory and running 4.4x faster, and ships with a dedicated inference runtime.
takeaways: Replacing linear layers with ternary-weight, 8-bit-activation layers removes most floating-point multiply-accumulates, opening the door to specialized edge accelerators.
A full-precision teacher aligning the quantized vision encoder's latents helps preserve accuracy after compression.
A dedicated runtime with packed ternary weights ran 3.52x faster than PyTorch on the same GPU.

talks.title: EagleVLA: Towards Onboard Real-Time Robot Control via Foresight-Aligned Asynchronous Inference
talks.summary: The authors target VLA deployment on low-power onboard devices like Jetson Orin, where long inference causes perception-execution misalignment and slow reactions. They predict future VLM hidden states from committed actions so the action expert acts from the future timestep, schedule VLM versus action-expert calls by prediction confidence, and add an onboard inference engine.
takeaways: Asynchronous inference alone hides latency but leaves the robot acting on stale observations; predicting the future representation corrects this.
Confidence-based scheduling lets the cheap action expert run alone when future predictions are reliable, cutting reaction time.
Real-world cloth folding showed smoother trajectories than synchronous inference and real-time chunking baselines.

talks.title: REACT: Rolling Denoising and Dual Decoupling for Reactive Robot Control with VLA Models
talks.summary: REACT addresses the trade-off between smooth long action chunks and reactive replanning in flow-based VLAs by keeping a rolling action buffer whose blocks sit at staggered denoising stages, refined with each fresh observation. Dual decoupling runs sensing, VLM encoding, denoising and execution asynchronously.
takeaways: Faster inference or async execution alone does not raise 'input throughput', the rate at which fresh observations influence actions.
Rolling denoising lets each executed block be refined across several recent observations, improving smoothness and responsiveness together.
Training with staggered per-block noise levels gave faster convergence and lower open-loop prediction error.

talks.title: TARC: Time-Adaptive Robotic Control
talks.summary: TARC is an RL framework in which the policy outputs both an action and how long to hold it, under a budget on control updates, so control frequency becomes learned. On a quadruped the rate stays low when standing and spikes when pushed, and on a pi-0 VLA it adaptively decides when to replan.
takeaways: The constrained problem reduces to a standard MDP with a per-update cost, so any off-the-shelf RL algorithm applies.
TARC matched a fixed 50 Hz policy at under half the control rate, while a fixed-rate policy at the same average rate performed worse.
Adaptive replanning on pi-0 kept the same success rate while saving about 38% of forward passes.

talks.title: Diffusion ReRoll: Revisable Denoising for Robotic Sequential Prediction
talks.summary: Diffusion ReRoll selectively re-noises regions of a sequence that have stabilized while others keep denoising, letting earlier and later parts of a horizon revise each other. It is evaluated on OGBench planning, LIBERO/RoboCasa policy learning, unified video-action prediction and real-world navigation with 5 Hz onboard inference.
takeaways: Full-sequence diffusion can commit to a wrong decision and just make it cleaner, and causal diffusion forcing cannot let later context revise an early prefix.
Gains from re-noising grow with the number of re-noising events until they saturate, and causal attention masks limit the benefit.
In real navigation it handled out-of-distribution layouts and sharp turns where full-sequence and causal baselines failed.

talks.title: Targeting World Models to Compromise Robot Learning Pipelines
talks.summary: The authors show that world models used to generate synthetic robot training data are a stealthy poisoning entry point: imperceptible image perturbations to safe-looking demonstrations can inject malicious prompts into text-conditioned models or backdoor the dynamics of action-conditioned models. The poisoned rollouts then propagate into VLA and PPO policies.
takeaways: Perturbing a context frame could make a text-conditioned world model generate a different, harmful task (e.g., placing a weapon in a gift box) from a benign prompt.
A backdoor makes the world model's predictions collapse unless the agent takes a target action when it sees a trigger, which an RL policy then learns.
The authors call this the first backdoor attack injected solely by attacking a world model and urge more secure world-model supply chains.

talks.title: Chunk-wise Model-based Policy Optimization
talks.affiliation: Zhejiang University / Shanghai Innovation Institute / Westlake University
talks.summary: The authors replace recurrent world-model rollouts with a chunk world model that maps a latent state and a predicted action chunk to a future latent chunk in one pass, optimizing value expansion without backpropagation through time. They evaluate on HumanoidBench and deploy bipedal walking on a Unitree Go2 quadruped.
takeaways: Chunk-level prediction avoids compounding one-step errors and the instability of gradients through recurrent rollouts.
On HumanoidBench it reached strong performance with about 50% of the training time and 30x faster inference than TD-MPC2.
The method discovered bipedal walking on a real quadruped faster than SAC.
author_affiliations: Zhejiang University / Shanghai Innovation Institute / Westlake University
Shanghai Innovation Institute / Shanghai Jiao Tong University

talks.title: FedGuide: Diffusion Prior Alignment and Value Baseline Guidance for Heterogeneous Federated Reinforcement Learning
talks.summary: FedGuide tackles federated RL across clients with different dynamics, rewards and initial states by using personalized diffusion priors aggregated through an optimal-transport mixture of experts, plus a DICE value baseline to stabilize prior-regularized PPO. It is evaluated on MuJoCo locomotion and Meta-World manipulation.
takeaways: Directly averaging local policies erases the specialized behavior modes each heterogeneous client needs.
Aggregating behavior priors in distribution space preserved multiple reward modes where policy averaging collapsed to one.
The DICE value baseline was credited with substantially lower return volatility across training rounds.

talks.title: MoRE: Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Physics Robotic World Models
talks.summary: MoRE is a 3D point-based world model that routes robot interactions to motion experts for rigid, deformable and prehensile dynamics on a shared encoder, trained on Isaac Sim and real data. Integrated with MPC, one model pushes rigid boxes, manipulates soft cloth and performs multi-step tool use on a real robot.
takeaways: A single shared dynamics model tends to blur distinct interaction regimes, which a mixture of experts with a router avoids.
MoRE improved prediction accuracy over prior methods across rigid, deformable and prehensile benchmarks.
Using one world model inside MPC enabled diverse real manipulation tasks without per-material models.

talks.title: Challenges to Realize Embodied AI
talks.summary: Introduced by Dieter Fox, Burgard frames robotics research as Sisyphus repeatedly pushing a boulder uphill with three technologies: probabilistic robotics, deep learning, and now foundation models. He credits probabilistic methods with millimeter-level localization and the rise of self-driving cars, but argues their reliance on HD maps confines systems to geofenced Level 4 autonomy, and that deep learning's need for predefined ontologies breaks down in messy homes. He then surveys foundation-model work from his groups on map-free navigation (FlowNav, MetricNet), LLM-chained skills, semantic grasping, tactile prediction, explicit wrench control, and interpretability of vision-language navigation agents. He closes with calls for calibrated uncertainty, force and touch in robot foundation models, shared large-scale academic compute, and a 'CERN of robotics'.
takeaways: Combining deep perception with probabilistic state estimation requires calibrated uncertainties, which becomes even harder with foundation models.
Burgard expects robots to reach factory floors much sooner than messy homes, mirroring how self-driving succeeded in more structured settings.
Map-free navigation still needs some metric geometry, as diffusion-based navigation without scale led to collisions that MetricNet's scaled waypoints fixed.
Adding explicit force/wrench control to imitation policies substantially improved contact-rich task performance over position-plus-stiffness control.
State-of-the-art vision-language navigation agents had under 70% precision against human-annotated relevant regions, motivating more interpretability work.
He argues academia must pool resources on open robot foundation models that include force and touch to keep pace with industry.

talks.title: Innovations in Autonomy at GM
talks.summary: Harris describes GM's shift from the Cruise robotaxi program to personal autonomy, targeting an eyes-off highway product in 2028. He contrasts self-play RL in a simulator running more than 50,000x real time, which surpasses human performance and learns recovery but uses simplified inputs and may not feel human, with imitation learning on hundreds of thousands of hours of driving logs. He sketches ways to combine them and describes on-car and offboard VLM uses such as scene reasoning, data mining, triage and critique.
takeaways: Robust merging and yielding behaviors emerged from under two hours of self-play training in GM's fast simulator.
Self-play gives coverage of rare events and avoids the DAgger compounding-error problem, while imitation gives realistic distributions and human-like behavior.
Possible combinations include anchoring RL to an imitation policy, distilling an RL teacher, or learning rewards from human driving.
VLMs are useful for high-level lane-level reasoning at crash scenes and for mining rare, unstructured events like road debris.

talks.title: RoboCap & RoboColosseum
talks.summary: Cho presents BitRobot's aim of crowdsourcing real-world data, including the RoboCap six-camera head-mounted capture device, wirelessly synced wrist cameras, tactile-glove integration, and open datasets such as RoboCap 10K, a LiDAR ground-truth set, a large urban navigation set and 500 hours of humanoids in real homes. Duan then introduces RoboColosseum, a large real-world evaluation effort with hundreds of robots, a 30-person evaluation team and hundreds of environments, offering fine-tune and open tracks.
takeaways: RoboCap 10K offers 10,000 hours of in-the-wild occupational work collected across 11 countries with hand pose and SLAM.
RoboColosseum's first evaluations found no model dominates every setting and no humanoid model reached full success.
Duan reports that roughly 400 to 500 comparisons are needed to draw statistically significant conclusions about models.
RoboColosseum is offering 10,000 hours of free real-world evaluation to academic labs.

talks.title: Data Infrastructure for Physical AI
talks.summary: MaxInsights' co-founder and CTO presents the company as a large provider of egocentric human data for robot learning, with over two million hours delivered. He shares internal evidence of data quality, a pre-training run using only egocentric data reaching success rates similar to a model trained on about ten times more mixed data, and a fine-grained language annotation scheme with per-hand, phase-level labels. He also previews an open annotation dataset and an in-the-wild evaluation and correction feedback loop.
takeaways: Pre-training on about 600 hours of their egocentric data was reported to roughly match a baseline trained on over 6,000 hours of robot plus egocentric data in simulation.
Language annotations are structured around goal clarity, temporal consistency and execution detail, labeled separately for left and right hands at about one-second granularity.
MaxInsights plans to open-source an annotation dataset with finger-level contact labels, which it says existing egocentric datasets lack.
A reasoning model that checks outcomes and sends corrective feedback to the policy is part of its real-world data feedback loop.

talks.title: Ego2Robot: Scalable Robot Data Synthesis from Egocentric Human Data
talks.affiliation: Renmin University of China / Alibaba Inc.
talks.summary: The authors present Ego2Robot, a pipeline that converts egocentric human manipulation videos into robot training data by retargeting hand poses to gripper actions, inpainting human arms, replaying motion in simulation and overlaying the rendered robot onto the original scene, then filtering low-quality clips. They use an extended RoboTwin benchmark to measure how this synthetic data helps pre-train robot foundation models along appearance, scene layout, embodiment and task-semantics axes.
takeaways: A balanced mix of synthesized Ego2Robot data and real robot data works best for pre-training, and mixing in synthesized robot-format data beats mixing in the raw egocentric videos.

The largest gains appear for lighting and robot-color variation, camera-shift robustness, cross-embodiment transfer and instructions involving unseen objects, and adding more robot bodies keeps improving transfer.
Hand-pose estimation accuracy currently limits gains on the most precise real-robot tasks.

talks.title: Learning Human Intention for Robotic Manipulation
talks.summary: The authors use human gaze as an embodiment-agnostic signal of intention: a model pre-trained on a large egocentric dataset annotated with hand and gaze first predicts intention tokens autoregressively and then generates actions, in a chain-of-thought style. Post-training needs only a small amount of robot data without gaze annotations, paired with on-task human data.
takeaways: High-level intention transfers across embodiments far more easily than low-level actions, so it serves as a bridge for human-to-robot transfer.
Manually editing the predicted intention changes the robot's trajectory on the fly, and modeling intention raises task success.
Human data helps in both pre-training and post-training and lets the robot succeed in scenarios seen only in human videos.
