talks.title: Efficient and Reliable Teleoperation through Real-to-Sim-to-Real Shared Autonomy
talks.summary: The authors propose a real-to-sim-to-real shared-autonomy framework in which a residual RL co-pilot, trained in simulation against a k-nearest-neighbor human surrogate fitted to under five minutes of real teleoperation, assists operators in contact-rich tasks such as nut threading, gear meshing and peg insertion. The human supplies high-level intent while the co-pilot handles low-level contact alignment.
takeaways: Splitting roles, with the human giving intent and RL handling low-level contact control, makes teleoperation more reliable without solving full autonomy.
Co-pilot-assisted teleoperation raises success, cuts completion time and workload, and follows operator intent such as varying insertion speed.
Diffusion policies trained on co-pilot-assisted demonstrations outperform those trained on the same amount of direct teleoperation data.

talks.title: FlowDAgger: Human-in-the-Loop Adaptation of Generative Robot Policies in Latent Space
talks.summary: Michael Murray presents FlowDAgger, which adapts frozen flow-matching and diffusion policies (such as pi0.5, Cosmos Policy and plain diffusion policies) from a handful of human space-mouse corrections by training a small latent-steering policy. Its key ingredient is action inversion: a fixed-point optimization maps each correction back to the noise latent that would produce it, used inside a DAgger-style loop.
takeaways: Supervising the latent space directly with inverted corrections makes progress in tens of episodes, whereas exploring noise space can take thousands.
Because only a small latent policy is trained, the method preserves the pre-trained prior and avoids the catastrophic forgetting seen with supervised fine-tuning, and it runs on a consumer GPU.
Gains are largest on tasks with high-precision bottlenecks.

talks.title: BiDexGrasp: Coordinated Bimanual Dexterous Grasps across Object Geometries and Sizes
talks.summary: The authors introduce BiDexGrasp, a bimanual dexterous grasp synthesis pipeline and generative model. Region-based initialization and decoupled optimization make synthesis 40 times faster and produce a dataset of nearly 10 million grasps, while a bimanual coordination module and object-adaptive grasp anchors handle coordination and large size variation.
takeaways: Initializing both hands in promising regions and decoupling their optimization makes bimanual grasp synthesis far more efficient, more than doubling the baseline synthesis success rate.
The learned generator improves success by about 25 percentage points over the baseline.
In real tests it reaches 74.6% success over 260 trials on 30 objects, including transfer to other robot hands.

talks.title: KPGrasp: Scalable Keypoint Flow Matching for Dexterous Grasp Generation
talks.summary: KPGrasp represents dexterous grasps as 3D hand keypoints in the object frame and trains a DiT-style transformer with only the standard flow-matching loss, recovering joint angles with a lightweight inverse-kinematics step and no contact losses or test-time refinement.
takeaways: On Dexonomy it reaches 76.3% success with 2.4 mm penetration and transfers zero-shot to DexGraspAnything at 63.8% success.
An all-Euclidean keypoint parameterization avoids kinematic error accumulation, simplifies loss balancing and scales better with data, model and batch size.
Real-world grasping from single-view partial point clouds succeeds in 83 of 100 trials across 20 objects.

talks.title: WM-Craftnet: World Synesthesia Model for Robust and Generalizable Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation
talks.summary: WM-Craftnet trains a Dreamer-style recurrent state-space world model on depth, touch, proprioception, past actions and rewards for a 20-DoF humanoid hand. Its latent state, trained to reconstruct clean depth from noisy sensors, conditions a closed-loop in-hand rotation policy instead of being used for imagination.
takeaways: Clean-depth reconstruction regularizes noisy sensing and improves sim-to-real robustness, while deployment uses only the raw sensors.
A world model pre-trained on just nine objects serves as a reusable prior that lets a downstream policy generalize to 49 objects without object identifiers or privileged information.
Recurrent history estimates the current contact state, enabling recovery from disturbances and re-centering from difficult initial grasps.

talks.title: Sequential Asymmetric Imitation for Learning Coupled Robot Policies
talks.summary: The authors propose Sequential Asymmetric Imitation (SAI), which lets a single teleoperator train coupled policies for two bimanual mobile manipulators: robot A is first learned with a human partner, robot B is then taught alongside A's frozen policy, and A is fine-tuned on corrections where it must wait, yield or recover. Tasks include spreading a tablecloth and turning a painting upright.
takeaways: Making the learned partner part of the teaching process lets B adapt to A's actual timing and mistakes, without synchronized dual-operator demonstrations.
SAI beats independently trained imitation policies with the same architecture and budget, mainly by learning when to wait and how to keep shared support.
Message-passing baselines do well with reliable communication but degrade under delay and packet loss.
author_affiliations: Zeno AI / The University of Sydney

talks.title: Leave It Better Than Found: Value-Guided Cooperation in Sequential Tasks
talks.summary: Mario Gomez Andreu presents PAVE, an ad hoc method for sequential task continuation in which a leader robot optimizes online a trade-off between its own objective and the follower's value function at the handoff state, using its own policy as a prior. An out-of-distribution indicator stops the leader from trusting the follower's value in states the follower never saw in training.
takeaways: Sharing an RL follower's existing value function enables cooperation without joint training data, which matters when robots come from different makers.
Follower value estimates are overconfident out of distribution, so gating them with an OOD indicator is essential.
The method raises follower success by about 28 percentage points while keeping leader success high, and it matches a privileged fine-tuning baseline.

talks.title: RL Token: Bootstrapping Online RL with Vision-Language-Action Models
talks.summary: Charles Xu presents RL Token from Physical Intelligence, which adapts a pi0.6 VLA to expose a single compressed 'RL token', learned via an encoder-decoder that must reconstruct the full final-layer embeddings, as the observation for a small online actor-critic. The actor is conditioned on the VLA's sampled action chunk and regularized toward it, and online RL with human success labels and interventions targets only the hardest part of a task, such as aligning a screwdriver or threading a zip tie.
takeaways: The VLA's pre-trained embeddings are a far better perception backbone for small-network RL than generic encoders; swapping from a ResNet-10 to the RL token roughly doubled downstream RL speed in ablations.
Conditioning the Gaussian RL actor on the VLA's action proposal avoids collapsing to the mean of a multimodal flow policy and eases learning.
On Ethernet insertion the RL policy's median episode is 66 steps, versus 230 for SFT and about 150 for an expert teleoperator, and half its episodes beat the fastest teleop episode.
Targeted online RL on a task's bottleneck takes hours rather than the days needed for full-VLA iterative RL.

talks.title: Flow Policy Gradients for Robot Control
talks.summary: Hongsuk Choi presents FPO++, which makes flow-matching policy-gradient RL (FPO) stable for robot control through two changes: per-sample trust regions that clip each noise-timestep ratio, and an asymmetric trust region that keeps PPO clipping for positive advantages and uses SPO for negative ones. The method trains locomotion and humanoid motion tracking from scratch and deployed on real robots, and fine-tunes image-based manipulation policies.
takeaways: Original FPO collapsed on complex robotics tasks; per-sample clipping plus asymmetric trust regions yield consistent, high returns across seeds and thresholds.
Pushing the flow away from negative-advantage actions can inflate the ELBO posterior gap, which SPO-style regularization prevents.
Flow policies learn semantically meaningful joint correlations and preserve exploration longer than Gaussian PPO, producing more natural gaits.
Zero-noise sampling at inference gives smoother and more reliable actions even with few integration steps.
author_affiliations: UC Berkeley / The University of Hong Kong

talks.title: Driving, Fast or Slow? Neuro-Symbolic Guidance for Motion Prediction in Multi-Modal Ground Mobility
talks.summary: Simon Kohaut and Felix Divo present TraCS (Trajectory Compliance-Shaping), which fuses the proposals of black-box motion forecasters with a probabilistic first-order-logic model of local traffic rules via a log-linear opinion pool, with a learned trust gate deciding when rules apply. An agentic loop of coder, judge and verifier translates natural-language traffic rules into Resin probabilistic logic programs that can be evaluated in milliseconds.
takeaways: Frontier LLMs as coding agents translated the rule texts into correct programs, with the judge and verifier mattering more for weaker models.
On Argoverse 2 with QCNet, DeMo and other backbones the overall gains are small but concentrate in the highest-error tail, especially for pedestrians.
Always applying rules or shuffling the learned trust weights does not help, so knowing when agents follow rules is as important as the rules themselves.
Rule violations and mispredictions flagged by the compliance landscape can guide future data collection.
author_affiliations: TU Darmstadt / hessian.AI / Centre for Cognitive Science / DFKI

talks.title: Learning Without Starting Over: Expanding What Robots Can Learn in the Real World
talks.summary: Introduced by Georgia Chalvatzaki, Martin-Martin argues that because no robot can be pre-trained for every future, what matters is a robot's 'learning potential': how much new capability it gains from limited real-world experience. Starting from a baby-banging-to-hammering experiment, he shows that the way prior knowledge is reused determines what can still be learned. He then surveys lab work on learned action spaces for safe real-world RL (SLAC, mode-indexed diffusion policies), extracting structure from human demos and corrections (SafeMimic, OopsieVerse damage simulation, Oopsie-Recover), and choosing which data to train on or collect (DataMIL, GUILD). He closes with memory and continual learning via experience logs, grounded human feedback and LoRA-adapted VLAs.
takeaways: Fine-tuning a self-supervised banging skill learns hammering faster than learning from scratch, while freezing it learns fastest but plateaus, so the form of reuse matters as much as the prior.
A task-agnostic, safety-biased latent action space learned in simulation let mobile manipulators learn contact-rich tasks with under one hour of real-world RL and almost no safety interruptions.
A handful of language-annotated corrections turned into gated programmatic costs improved a frozen VLA by about 35%, and about 20% in new situations.
Selecting co-training data by its predicted effect on the target policy beats image or language similarity heuristics, and even helps a robot not present in Open X-Embodiment.
Sequential LoRA adapters with on-policy RL let a VLA gain new skills with near-zero average forgetting, making it a promising substrate for continual learning.
Learned safety offers probabilistic rather than formal guarantees, so future evaluation will rely on testing how safe policies are.

talks.title: EgoScale: Scaling Dexterous Manipulation with Diverse Egocentric Human Data
talks.summary: Ruijie Zheng presents EgoScale, which pre-trains a GR00T-style VLA on large-scale egocentric human video converted to actions via SLAM and hand-pose estimation and retargeted to a 22-DoF Sharpa hand, then mid-trains on aligned human and robot data (about 4 hours of teleop paired with 50 hours of glove- and wrist-camera-tracked human data on the same tasks) before post-training on new dexterous tasks.
takeaways: Combining human pre-training with aligned mid-training gives the highest success on five dexterous tasks, and only this combination achieves non-trivial success on the hardest ones such as bottle unscrewing and syringe transfer.
Human validation loss follows a log-linear scaling law in the amount of human data and correlates with real-robot performance.
One-shot transfer emerges: a new task such as shirt folding is learned from a single teleop trajectory plus about 100 human demonstrations.
The same recipe transfers to a Unitree G1 with a different hand, with smoother motions than the baselines.

talks.title: OPENDEXGRASP: Open-vocabulary Task-Oriented Dexterous Grasping
talks.summary: OpenDexGrasp generates task-oriented dexterous grasps from free-form language instructions. It combines OpenDex-Scale (1.24 million synthesized grasps labeled with task descriptions by a VLM) with OpenDex-Align (about 27k human-demonstrated functional grasps transferred across object instances), and a model that couples a pre-trained VLM with a 3D geometry encoder and jointly predicts task affordance and hand pose.
takeaways: Pairing broad synthetic coverage with smaller high-quality human-aligned data improves both physical and functional grasp quality.
Predicting affordance alongside the grasp ties the language instruction to where the hand should make contact.
Replacing the pre-trained VLM backbone causes the largest drop in ablations, and real-robot grasps succeed 72% of the time.
Remaining failures involve objects whose pose must be changed substantially before a functional grasp is possible.
author_affiliations: Peking University / Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence
Peking University / Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence

talks.title: Play2Perfect: What Matters in Dexterous Play Pretraining for Precise Assembly?
talks.summary: Tyler Lum and Kushal Kedia present Play2Perfect, in which a multi-fingered hand is first pre-trained with RL on 'play', reaching random 6D goal poses with thousands of random objects, and then fine-tuned with a sparse CAD-defined reward for precise long-horizon assembly such as half-millimeter insertions and screwing a table leg. Policies are trained entirely in simulation and deployed zero-shot with FoundationPose object tracking.
takeaways: With play pre-training, assembly reaches high success within 2 to 5 hours of fine-tuning, while RL from scratch stays at 0% after 24 hours and dense-reward RL takes 33 times longer to match it.
Play-pretrained policies grasp with multiple fingers and stay above 80% success under force perturbations, whereas dense-reward RL learns brittle strategies that fail.
Effective play requires full 6D (not translation-only) goals, tight 1 cm tolerances, many objects and fresh random goals each episode, all of which emphasize in-hand manipulation.
Play alone handles free-space motion but fails at contact; fine-tuning teaches contact-rich search strategies, and small objects remain hard due to occlusion.

talks.title: FACTR 2: Learning External Force Sensing for Commodity Robot Arms Improves Policy Learning
talks.summary: Jason Liu and Steven Oh present FACTR 2, which gives low-cost arms external force sensing with NEXT: an LSTM trained in about one minute on roughly 10 minutes of free-space joint positions, velocities and motor currents predicts free-space torque, so the residual during contact is the external torque. This estimate drives force-feedback teleoperation on arms like Piper, YAM and Nero, and FIRST uses it to segment demos into free, pre-contact and contact phases and up-sample the latter two during behavior-cloning training.
takeaways: On a Franka, NEXT estimates track the built-in torque sensors during contact and stay near zero in free motion.
Using external torque both as a policy input and to resample pre-contact and contact segments gave the best results on long-horizon tasks such as belt assembly.
Up-sampling contact phases lowers validation loss there and produces more recovery behavior when alignment fails.
About 10 minutes of free-motion data was enough, as 30 to 40 minutes did not improve performance.

talks.title: PACE: Temporal-Role Tactile Conditioning for Chunk-Based Insertion Policies
talks.summary: Presented by Zane on behalf of first author Zhiyuan Chen (Xiaomi Robotics), who could not attend due to visa delays. PACE gives a shared tactile stream three temporal roles in a chunk-based insertion policy: a phase pathway that modulates transformer features from smoothed contact state, an event pathway that gates a residual correction to the first actions of the chunk on abrupt contact changes, and an auxiliary future-tactile prediction head used only in training. Demonstrations were collected with a Sigma.7 force-feedback teleoperation system.
takeaways: PACE reaches 90.7% average success over five real insertion tasks versus 46% for the strongest tactile-concatenation baseline, and 88.7% on Manipulation-Net including tight 0.1 mm clearance.
The event pathway contributes most, since removing it drops success to 66.7%.
Force feedback during teleoperation reduced average peak contact force from 16.7 N to 10 N.
The design transfers across sensors (force-torque, joint currents) and backbones such as diffusion policy.

talks.title: Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions
talks.summary: Kallol Saha presents DISCO, an AlphaGo-style recipe for long-horizon multi-object rearrangement: a pick-and-place policy proposes actions as edges in an MCTS tree over continuous actions using progressive widening, and successes and failures are periodically distilled back into the policy and a value function, run in parallel in GPU simulation. The final policies run without search at test time on shelf-packing, stacking and table-bussing tasks, including sim-to-real transfer.
takeaways: Progressive widening, adding children as nodes are visited more, makes tree search tractable over continuous action spaces.
DISCO outperforms beam search, MPPI, RL and ablations with uniform search or a fixed branching factor.
Both the policy and the value function improve each distillation round, so long-horizon reasoning is learned from short-horizon data.
A behavior-cloning-only initial policy fails on real long-horizon tasks that the distilled DISCO policy completes.

talks.title: GRAIL: Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from World Models
talks.summary: The authors propose generating humanoid loco-manipulation data instead of collecting it: starting from a single image of a constructed 3D scene, text prompts drive a video foundation model to produce human demonstrations (sitting, pushing, carrying, climbing stairs, stepping onto curbs). Human and object motion is reconstructed using the privileged scene geometry and camera parameters, retargeted to robots by choosing a human character with matching height, and made physically valid with a scene- and terrain-aware whole-body tracker. A visual policy distilled from these trackers and trained entirely in simulation is deployed zero-shot on real humanoids.
takeaways: GRAIL generated over 35k physically valid motions, and the public dataset had about a quarter of a million downloads at the time of the talk.
A pickup policy trained only on GRAIL data transferred zero-shot to the real robot with 80% success on unseen objects.
Generating thousands of staircase variants virtually gives terrain coverage that motion capture cannot practically achieve, and the stair policy generalized to unseen indoor and outdoor stairs.
The authors still retarget from human videos because video models and pose estimators are mature for humans, but they expect direct humanoid video generation once both are fine-tuned for robots.

talks.title: SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model
talks.summary: SuperMimic scales general humanoid motion tracking by learning one differentiable world model of the dynamics shared across all motions, fit from simulator transitions, and training the tracking policy through it with first-order gradients (SHAC-style) plus a critic, in a single alternating loop. Liao shows a live demo of the world model and tracker reacting to perturbations, and argues that amortizing one model across motions keeps model error flat as data grows. The resulting general tracker transfers to a real Unitree G1 despite being trained in imagination.
takeaways: Liao reports training a general tracker in about three hours on one GPU, versus over 100 GPUs for a week for SONIC, roughly a thousandfold reduction in GPU hours, while acknowledging a smaller dataset and faster GPU.
Imagination rollouts are over 10x faster than simulation, and first-order gradients through the model need far fewer steps than PPO on the same model.
With longer training the method reached zero tracking failures across about 100,000 motions.
The code was open-sourced during the talk; others had already reimplemented and extended it to speed-runs, muscle-driven humanoids, and sparse-reward manipulation without references.

talks.title: RoboNaldo: Accurate, Stable and Powerful Humanoid Soccer Shooting via Motion-Guided Curriculum Reinforcement Learning
talks.affiliation: Archon Robotics / The University of Hong Kong
talks.summary: RoboNaldo trains a single low-level humanoid policy for soccer shooting via a three-stage motion-guided curriculum: first tracking one human kick reference, then learning accurate shooting with sparse task rewards by initializing balls near the tracked strike, and finally unifying locomotion and shooting with an adaptive reference anchored toward the ball and a heuristic planner for kick timing. Onboard LiDAR detects a reflective ball and a chest camera reads AprilTag targets on the goal, and the system was tested on a Unitree G1 across indoor and outdoor fields.
takeaways: Initializing the ball near the tracked strike makes the tracking policy a good starting point for PPO and solves the sparse-reward exploration problem.
Real-robot contact rates exceeded 90%, with 100% success on the stationary-ball kick condition reported in the talk.
Peak ball speed exceeded 10 m/s, which the speaker estimated at roughly 60% of a professional player's shot.
The sim-to-real gap remains the main source of failures, especially stability after the kick on outdoor fields.
author_affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
Archon Robotics / The University of Hong Kong

talks.title: Building general purpose robots with Gemini
talks.summary: Rao frames robotics' core problem as combining general-purpose reasoning with dexterous whole-body control, attacked from both frontier models and robot models. He recaps Gemini Robotics 2.0 (whole-body control of the Apollo humanoid, dexterous hands, multi-robot collaboration) and announces Gemini Robotics 2.5, trained on 200+ tasks, with improved safety and a Mercedes-Benz/Apptronik production-line kitting pilot. He also announces MuJoCo 4 and MuJoCo Playground 1.0, and describes using frontier Gemini models as agents to build simulators from real logs, analyze rollouts, and even teach a humanoid to play cornhole.
takeaways: Training across 200+ dexterous tasks lifted success by roughly 30-100% over the previous model, and previously learned tasks also improved.
The production-line kitting pilot reached 96% autonomous success.
Frontier models are now accelerating robot model development through real-to-sim-to-real loops and automated failure analysis, and were used in building Gemini Robotics 2.5.
Rao predicts frontier models will take over more of robotics and that agentic, closed-loop robot control will arrive as these models get faster.

talks.title: Actions and Agents for True Long-Horizon Behavior.
talks.summary: Rodriguez reports on an early deployment of Atlas at Hyundai's Savannah plant doing part sequencing: picking parts from supplier containers, scanning barcodes bimanually, inserting them into the correct slots in order, and discarding dropped or defective parts. The system uses a cloud 'job harness' built around a fine-tuned Gemini ER reasoning model (system 2) that reads a text job description and factory tasking, and a single on-robot action model on an NVIDIA Thor (system 1), post-trained on about 400 hours of teleoperation data. He argues for a single action model over skill decomposition and for data quality over scale.
takeaways: End-to-end completion was 98.6% including interventions, with a 9.5% intervention rate, about one intervention every 20 minutes.
Cycle time is about two minutes per task, roughly 50% slower than the one-per-minute rate needed for economic value; Boston Dynamics predicts Atlas's first 8-hour production shift in 2027.
No off-the-shelf frontier VLM was reliable enough for task-completion checking and slot-precise steering without fine-tuning.
Rodriguez sees large-scale RL in simulation as a path to high-quality data, showing emergent dexterous behaviors from RGB-only policies.

talks.title: The Reference Platform for Physical AI
talks.summary: Parusel describes Franka's goal of being the reference hardware and software platform for physical AI research, building on the torque-sensing 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arm and its 1 kHz Franka Control Interface. He introduces the FR3 Duo dual-arm system and a new mobile FR3 Duo with a holonomic base, along with a range of teleoperation interfaces. He also highlights Franka's recently open-sourced data pipeline covering teleoperation, sensor capture, labeling, training and inference, and the DualBench benchmark paper.
takeaways: Over 2,000 publications in a single year used Franka robots, and at CoRL 2024 over half of single-arm papers used them.
Joint torque sensing and full model access (Jacobians, mass matrix) via a high-rate interface are the features Parusel credits for contact-rich and HRI research use.
A standardized dual-arm configuration with fixed cameras and grippers is meant to let labs reproduce each other's work and pool data on a common embodiment.
Franka released its data collection and training pipeline as open source and invites contributions of new input devices and labeling tools.

talks.title: DeTac: Dual-branch Decoupling of Texture and Force Signals in Vision-Based Tactile Sensors
talks.summary: DeTac is a dual-branch generative framework that separates marker images and clean shading from a single marker-based vision tactile sensor image, using a diffusion shading branch and a lightweight marker branch with cross-branch losses, trained on real paired data.
takeaways: Concurrent dual-branch decoupling avoids the mask-sizing dilemma and error accumulation of serial mask-then-inpaint pipelines.
Removing marker interference let a fabric classifier trained on marker-free data correctly classify marker-based sensor images.

talks.title: FingerEye: Learning Dexterous Manipulation with Continuous Vision-Tactile Sensing
talks.summary: FingerEye is a fingertip sensor with two cameras behind a transparent compliant plate that provides vision before contact and tactile cues after, paired with a policy that encodes each observation group separately and reads them through per-group attention.
takeaways: Binocular fingertip views improved success by 10 percentage points over a single camera.
Attention diagnostics showed naive fusion over-relies on easy global cues, motivating separate modality pathways.
author_affiliations: RoboScience / Huazhong University of Science and Technology
RoboScience / South China University of Technology

talks.title: DAVATaR: Depth-Aware Visually Augmented Tactile Learning Across the Air-Water Interface
talks.summary: DAVATaR tackles manipulation across the air-water interface with a waterproof gripper that transmits fingertip pressure fluidically to electronics above water, combined with immersion-depth sensing and visual augmentations for glare, occlusion and refraction in a multimodal transformer policy.
takeaways: Adding immersion-depth sensing raised success from 25% to 61% on a task where vision alone could not recover the state.
Tactile sensing alone is not enough when vision is heavily distorted, especially under water-level variation.

talks.title: Visible Touch: Rendering Contact for Visuomotor Policies
talks.summary: Visible Touch renders readings from a low-cost magnetic tactile sensor as arrows overlaid on camera images, so existing image-based policies and VLAs can be fine-tuned with contact information without architectural changes.
takeaways: The overlay lifted a pretrained MiniVLA from about 51% to 79.8% average success, with larger gains on multi-grasp long-horizon tasks.
On real tasks with pi-0.5, multi-arrow overlays beat feeding a separate tactile camera view.

talks.title: Demystifying When and Why VLAs Fail in Contact-Rich Tasks and How to Fix Them
talks.summary: The authors trace VLA failures in contact-rich tasks to precision failures, caused by the flow-matching noise schedule underweighting small near-contact actions, and force failures; they fix the first by switching to a logit-normal noise schedule and the second with time-aware, contact-gated force injection.
takeaways: Swapping the beta schedule for a logit-normal one at post-training is a drop-in fix with no extra parameters or data.
Across 2,500 real rollouts on five tasks the method reached 66% success, 25 points above the best baseline.

talks.title: Never Too Late for Force: Accelerating VLA Post-Training with Reactive Force Injection
talks.affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Shanghai Innovation Institute
talks.summary: LIFT adds force awareness to a pretrained VLA during post-training by grafting a reactive action expert with force memory that updates actions within each chunk, initialized to preserve pretrained knowledge, with force data gathered through online DAgger.
takeaways: Force history, not just the current reading, is needed to tell an ongoing insertion from a completed one.
Late, zero-initialized force injection kept the VLA's visual generalization to new objects, tablecloths and lighting.
author_affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Shanghai Innovation Institute
Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Shanghai Innovation Institute
Shanghai Innovation Institute / Southern University of Science and Technology

Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Shanghai Innovation Institute / Noematrix Ltd.

talks.title: Constraint-Decomposed Impedance Control from Generative Policy for Articulated Object Manipulation
talks.summary: For articulated objects, the authors sample several trajectories from a generative policy at grasp closure, convert them to body twists, and use PCA to find the feasible motion subspace, then set high impedance gains along it and low gains elsewhere.
takeaways: Policy sampling diversity can be turned into direction-wise compliance without a model of the object.
On a real Franka the constraint-violating force impulse dropped about 72% and peak force about 70%.

talks.title: TAM: Torque Adaptation Module for Robust Motion Transfer in Manipulation
talks.summary: TAM is a lightweight module trained entirely in simulation that corrects low-level torque commands from recent motion history, so policies transfer across sim-to-real gaps, payloads and robot instances regardless of how they produce actions.
takeaways: Because all policies share the torque interface, one adapter improved box pushing, MPC ball balancing, behavior cloning and payload tracking.
A behavior-cloning policy trained only in simulation rose from 50% to 72% real-world success, nearly matching its simulated success rate.
author_affiliations: Allen Institute for AI / University of Toronto
Allen Institute for AI / University of Washington
Allen Institute for AI / University of Washington

talks.title: Combining Constrained Sampling and Reinforcement Learning for Manipulation
talks.affiliation: Technical University Berlin / Robotics Institute Germany / Fraunhofer HHI
talks.summary: Toussaint proposes moving RL's exploration problem into constrained sampling: physically feasible states (contacts, friction cones, static stability) are sampled from a first-principles constraint manifold and used as reset distributions and curricula for goal-conditioned manipulation policies.
takeaways: Constraint-sampled resets let RL learn in-hand cube reorientation with an upside-down hand, where naive resets flat-line.
Advances in Monte Carlo and manifold sampling should transfer directly to better RL exploration.
author_affiliations: Technical University Berlin / Robotics Institute Germany / Fraunhofer HHI

talks.title: Learning Physics-Guided Residual Dynamics for Deformable Object Simulation
talks.summary: PGRD combines an optimizable spring-mass simulator with a learned network that predicts residual corrections, modeling deformables like ropes and a duster with a rigid stem and soft feathers, and is used with MPPI for rope rerouting with goals generated from language via an image model.
takeaways: The hybrid kept a heterogeneous object's stem rigid while deforming its feathers, which pure spring-mass and learned baselines failed to do.
Generating goal images from natural language removes the need to specify deformable goals by hand.

talks.title: WireCraft: A Simulation Benchmark for Industrial DLO Manipulation
talks.summary: WireCraft is an Isaac-based benchmark for industrial deformable linear object manipulation with connector insertion, clip routing and channel seating tasks, configurable wire models, connector types and randomized geometry.
takeaways: Privileged-state policies insert reliably, but vision-based RL, imitation and VLA policies drop sharply, and tight-clearance insertion remains open.
Mixing simulation data into real demonstrations raised real insertion success from 15% to 80%.

talks.title: Enabling Robust Cloth Manipulation via Inference-Time Simulator-in-the-Loop Refinement
talks.affiliation: National University of Singapore / Shanghai Jiao Tong University
talks.summary: The authors use the FLASH cloth simulator as an inference-time forward model: a real-to-sim network recovers a cloth mesh from one RGB image, and MPPI refines a distilled policy's plan with 256 parallel rollouts before each executed action.
takeaways: The full system folded cloth successfully 90% of the time single-arm and 80% dual-arm, versus about 10-30% without refinement.
Simulator choice mattered: FLASH succeeded 95-100% in controlled comparisons while Isaac Sim and Newton stayed at or below 60%.
author_affiliations: National University of Singapore / Shanghai Jiao Tong University

talks.title: Robustness without Wrinkles: Parallel Simulation and Robust MPC for Certified Deformable Manipulation
talks.summary: CORD-SLS pairs a GPU-parallel differentiable deformable simulator with smoothed contact and a real-time robust output-feedback MPC, using conformal prediction to bound real-to-sim error, for certified rope and cloth manipulation.
takeaways: Contact smoothing yields gradients that also make analytic policy gradients converge in fewer steps than PPO.
On hardware the robust tubes gave zero obstacle collisions despite dynamics and measurement error.

talks.title: Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding for 3D Manipulation Policies under Depth Corruption
talks.summary: NISE learns spatial features for 3D manipulation policies directly from noisy depth, using cross-view supervision about which geometry is consistent across cameras and Gaussian-marginalized 3D attention that down-weights uncertain point positions.
takeaways: Under saturated depth noise NISE beat the strongest baseline by 33-40 percentage points across two simulation benchmarks.
On real transparent and reflective objects it roughly doubled baseline successes, for example 16 vs. 6 of 30 on a test-tube pouring task.

talks.title: SERF: Spatiotemporal Environment and Robot Feature Map for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
talks.summary: SERF conditions a VLA mobile manipulation policy on a spatiotemporal map of neural points for both the environment and the robot body, updated online via object-level rigid tracking and forward kinematics, and tokenized in multiple frames.
takeaways: Compared with an image-only pi-0.5 policy, the map-conditioned policy reached subgoals more directly and completed more of them.
An explicit 3D map gives the policy a mechanism to accumulate context that image-only foundation models lack.

talks.title: Articulated 3D Scene Graphs for Open-World Mobile Manipulation
talks.summary: MoMa-SG builds semantic-kinematic 3D scene graphs from RGB-D interaction videos by segmenting interactions, estimating articulations as twists from tracked points, and linking them to open-vocabulary objects, including items discovered inside containers.
takeaways: One regularized twist model robustly estimates both prismatic and revolute joints.
The graph supported long-horizon tasks on a Toyota HSR and a quadruped, such as opening a fridge and retrieving milk from a language command.

talks.title: RAM: Reachability Across Morphologies
talks.summary: RAM is a morphology-conditioned implicit neural model that predicts whether a pose is reachable, accounting for self-collisions, trained on 30 billion samples over 30,000 morphologies.
takeaways: RAM reached 84% balanced accuracy on unseen morphologies, beating learned IK by 15 points while running over 500x faster.
Being differentiable, it speeds up morphology optimization by more than an order of magnitude with comparable designs.
author_affiliations: German Electron Synchrotron / University of Hamburg

talks.title: Shape Your Body: Value Gradients for Multi-Embodiment Robot Design
talks.summary: The authors train one generalist locomotion policy and critic across 50 legged robots with heavy embodiment randomization, then freeze the critic and backpropagate through it to optimize design parameters.
takeaways: Training once replaces a new co-design RL run per design and allows thousands of designs to be optimized in seconds.
Optimized designs often beat the manufacturers' originals, and the value gradients show which parameters, such as actuator settings, limit performance.
author_affiliations: TU Darmstadt / Robotics Institute Germany / DFKI / hessian.AI

talks.title: Learning in the factories
talks.summary: Tedrake, introduced by Ani Majumdar, describes how founding Walden Robotics (a Toyota Research Institute spin-out started in January 2026) changed his view of robotics, arguing the technology is ready and that the next hurdle is turning general-purpose robots into products. He tells the story of Walden's first deployment, loading camshafts at a Toyota plant under strict uptime and safety requirements, using HG-DAGGER-style shared autonomy with remote assistants and weekly over-the-air model updates. He then argues that field deployment data is the most valuable data, presenting an experiment in which stronger pretrained models collected less intervention data yet improved more from it. He closes with runtime failure monitoring for few-to-many supervision, lessons from the Toyota Production System (jidoka, stopping the line, five whys), and manufacturing robots at scale with Toyota.
takeaways: Walden's camshaft deployment has never stopped the production line, because human remote assistance plus the AI reaches near-100% success.
After a recent large-model training run, mean time between interventions rose to about 340 seconds, which Tedrake estimates could let three remote assistants oversee 50 robots.

In shared-autonomy fine-tuning on new tasks, the strongest base model got the least intervention data back (about 1.36 hours versus about 2 hours for the weakest) but improved the most, so stronger base models make deployment data more valuable.
Autonomy ratio is a better metric for weak models and mean time between interventions is better for strong ones, because the nature of interventions changes as models improve.
Training only on intervention data misses root causes; Tedrake advocates Toyota-style post-mortem analysis and targeted data collection after failures.
He sees manufacturing robots at scale, not AI, as the current bottleneck, and pursues it by having robots build robots and partnering with Toyota for mass production.

talks.title: Building an Autonomous Humanoid for the Home
talks.summary: Tompson, modeling lead at Meta Robotics Studio, describes the team's goal of a home humanoid that is both useful (autonomous household tasks) and delightful (safe, friendly, communicative), built full-stack from actuators to frontier models. Without showing hardware, he outlines the modeling approach: a generalist dexterous foundation model trained on egocentric human data from Aria glasses, UMI-style data, and some robot teleoperation, refined with DAGGER. He argues Meta's existing assets (Quest SLAM and hand tracking, vision models like SAM 3 and SAM 3D, an FEM-based simulator, the Muse frontier model, and consumer hardware experience) give it an advantage.
takeaways: Meta reuses Quest headset SLAM and hand-tracking infrastructure directly on its robot.
Tompson now has strong conviction that simulation, including FEM simulation of cloth, sponges and fine rigid contact, is essential for general robotics.
Explicit vision models are gaining importance as tools that agents call for data filtering, QA and state estimation.
Meta is feeding robotics data into its frontier model and doing RL post-training to improve agentic tool calling for robot tasks.

talks.title: Scaling Robot Intelligence: From Human Experience to Self-Improving Robots
talks.summary: Shen presents AGIBOT's physical AI ecosystem grounded in deployment: over 20,000 robots produced in three years, including deployments in a tablet factory and more than 100 robots in the Guangzhou metro. He covers the open AgiBot World dataset (over 1 million trajectories, with new releases annotated for reasoning), AGIBOT's latest world-reasoning-action model, which combines task reasoning, future-state prediction and action generation and is trained on teleoperation plus egocentric human data, fleet-level collective experience learning across 96 robots, and Genie Master, which turns deployment experience into reusable memory. He closes with a community-built manipulation benchmark, which gained four new tracks that week and real-world validation of sim assets. Several demo videos failed to play during the talk.
takeaways: Collective experience learning ran on 96 physical robots at once, which AGIBOT believes is the first demonstration at this scale.
In a five-day convenience-store restocking experiment, Genie Master raised workflow success from 28.6% to 85.7%.
The benchmark's simulation assets are tuned to match the real world so that sim-to-real gaps can be measured, and it has around 20 contributing institutions and more than 190 teams using it.

talks.title: Building Foundational Models for Robotics at Tesla
talks.summary: Cho explains how Tesla uses learned world models to build robust policies, first for the Cybercab robotaxi and then for Optimus. Tesla uses the world models to evaluate counterfactuals after safety interventions, evaluate new policies in closed loop on collected scenarios, and train policies. The latter demands models that are causal, action-conditioned, multi-camera consistent, low-latency and physically accurate. He shows generated rare scenarios (falling branches, an elephant, driving through an aquarium) and Optimus locomotion and manipulation rollouts conditioned on joint-level actions and compared to ground truth.
takeaways: Using a world model for training, not just evaluation, raises the bar sharply because policies will exploit any physical inaccuracies.
Generating unseen tail scenarios is necessary because robotaxi interventions have become too rare to test against.
For Optimus, modeling the robot's own physics requires data from the target embodiment, which Tesla says motivates scaling Optimus production.
The world models are trained from scratch in-house so that they work like general video generators conditioned on the car's or robot's actual actions.

talks.title: RoboKit: Accelerating Parallel Differentiable Optimization for Robot Learning
talks.summary: The authors present RoboKit, a batched, kernel-level optimization toolkit with analytical Jacobians and multiple optimizers that covers IK, motion planning, retargeting, grasping and simulation-based MPC. They also compare optimization against learned solvers to show where neural methods help.
takeaways: RoboKit reports roughly 10x faster IK than prior frameworks, 2x faster physics retargeting, and 16x faster rendering-based calibration, solving 2,000 IK problems in about 70 ms.
For well-posed problems like IK and motion planning, optimization already performs well and learned methods only match it.
Learning helps when physics matters (sim-trained grasping), when inputs are partial point clouds, and when speed is critical (learned motion planning is hundreds of times faster).

talks.title: Control-Ready Uncertainty for Trajectory Diffusion
talks.summary: The authors introduce SCOPE, which reads the curvature of a diffusion model's score to produce trajectory uncertainty tubes without costly Monte Carlo sampling. These tubes are used as an MPPI policy prior and as forecasts of human motion for safer navigation and manipulation.
takeaways: Sharp score curvature means a tight trajectory distribution (narrow tube) and a flat score means a wide one, so uncertainty can come from a single learned module.
Used as a policy prior, SCOPE reduces MPPI collisions in narrow passages, and used as a forecast it makes the robot yield to pedestrians.
In a real pick-and-place with a human hand intruding, combining SCOPE as both prior and forecast let the robot back off early and finish the task.

talks.title: Emergent Control via Prior-Based Free Energy Minimization
talks.summary: The authors cast control as minimizing the squared deviation from prior (preferred) states, following the free energy principle, and evaluate model-based (Mountain Car, highway, goal reach) and model-free (Walker) variants against reward-based agents.
takeaways: The free-energy objective reaches PPO-comparable driving behavior and better long-horizon Walker stability than SAC, though with lower reward.
Unlike reward shaping, it is task-structure agnostic and succeeded on a reverse Mountain Car task where unshaped or wrongly shaped rewards failed.
It yields a denser optimization landscape and more noise robustness than unshaped RL in Mountain Car and goal reach, but not in Walker.

talks.title: GaP: A Graph-as-Policy Multi-Agent Self-Learning Harness For Variational Automation Tasks
talks.summary: GaP structures robot programs as computation graphs whose subgraphs are written, tested and repaired by coding agents, targeting variational automation tasks. The agent harness self-learns in simulation and can build real-to-sim environments from phone video.
takeaways: Structuring code as a graph keeps agent-written policies interpretable and lets them run on the robot without the agents in the loop.
Self-learning in simulation produced composite strategies, such as surveying, selecting, flipping and checking objects with only parallel-jaw grippers.
When sim physics mismatched reality, GaP used real-world video to update both the simulation and the graph (e.g., using the left gripper to stabilize a bar).

talks.title: Playful Agentic Robot Learning
talks.summary: The authors let an embodied coding agent team practice through self-directed play in simulation, proposing learnable tasks, writing and debugging control code, and storing successful routines in a frozen skill library for later, externally specified tasks.
takeaways: Play improved success on held-out LIBERO-Pro tasks by 20.6 percentage points over a no-play code agent, and by 17 points on a second benchmark.
The play-derived library transferred to another agent, adding 8.9 points on a separate benchmark.
Skills learned in simulation play, such as grasp selection and pull-direction helpers, composed into real-robot tasks like swapping two cubes without any real-world play or fine-tuning.

talks.title: Meta-Ctrl: Guaranteed Plan Generation by Decoupling Syntactic and Semantic Constraints
talks.summary: Meta-Ctrl is a constrained-decoding method that guarantees LLM-generated robot plans satisfy whole-plan rules, both preconditions and goal reachability. It computes, in one backward pass, the probability that a partial plan can still reach the goal, and tracks the world per action-level meta token while checking syntax separately.
takeaways: Per-step masks catch illegal actions but cannot stop plans that stall or never reach the goal, so look-ahead to the goal is needed.
Treating each action as one meta token and decoupling syntax from world state avoids a state explosion (about 350 million states and over 100 TB in token-level approaches).
On VirtualHome, Llama 3B rose from 20% to 90% success, and real-robot plans were valid 20/20 times versus about 2 for the unguided model.

talks.title: Bayesian Active Learning for Intent Disambiguation in Interactive Robot Planning
talks.summary: The authors use temporal logic (STL) as a shared representation linking intent clarification and planning. They maintain a Bayesian belief over task specifications, choose informative clarification questions via active learning, and then pass the inferred STL to a formal planner.
takeaways: Letting an LLM drive clarification alone produces superficial questions that can miss environmental context.
Sampling from a learned latent space of task specifications helps explore intents the LLM might overlook.
In a factory inspection scenario with a quadruped, the framework raised task success while asking fewer questions.

talks.title: ATOM-Bench: A Real-World Benchmark for Atomic Skills and Compositional Generalization in Manipulation Policies
talks.summary: ATOM-Bench is a real-world benchmark that fine-tunes policies only on atomic motor and instruction skills, then tests whether they can recombine those skills on held-out compositional tasks. It reports task completion, partial progress, atomic competence and diagnostic scores.
takeaways: The benchmark defines six motor-atom and seven instruction-atom types across Franka and a second robot platform.
Across five policies, simple instruction grounding is easiest, while precise motor control, counting and compositional generalization remain hard.
Policies that succeed at every individual atom can still fail when the atoms must be combined in a single task.

talks.title: Kamino: GPU-based Simulation of Rigid Multi-Body Physics with Kinematic Loops
talks.summary: Kamino is a GPU-based physics solver in NVIDIA's Newton framework for massively parallel simulation of rigid multi-body systems with kinematic loops. It is motivated by Disney's complex audio-animatronic figures, and the presenter's slides and video ran out of sync during the talk.
takeaways: Kamino uses a constrained maximal-coordinate formulation that handles kinematic loops, multi-contact coupling and large mass ratios while staying stable at large time steps.
It simulates thousands of heterogeneous worlds at once, so a single RL policy can control ant variants with different numbers of limbs.
Newton ships a public demo biped with six kinematic loops, and Kamino was validated against XPBD and MJWarp on analytical toy problems.

talks.title: PHUMA: Physically Reliable Humanoid Locomotion Dataset
talks.summary: PHUMA is a 73-hour humanoid locomotion dataset built from motion capture and internet video. Physically invalid motions are filtered out, and the rest are retargeted to G1 and H1 with physics-aware regularization.
takeaways: The authors argue that physical reliability matters as much as dataset size: small clean sets (LAFAN) and large noisy sets (Humanoid-X) both lag behind.
Retargeting penalizes joint-limit violations, floating, penetration and foot sliding.
PHUMA-trained trackers had the highest success on unseen motions, transferred zero-shot to hardware, and improved as more video data was added.

talks.title: LadderMan: Learning Humanoid Perceptive Ladder Climbing
talks.summary: LadderMan enables a humanoid to climb diverse ladders with perception and to manipulate while on the ladder. Expert policies trained with hybrid motion tracking from a single reference motion are distilled into one depth-based visuomotor policy.
takeaways: Relaxed upper-body tracking with ladder-centric contact and clinging rewards removes the need for large motion datasets.
A depth foundation model narrows the sim-to-real depth gap without heavy depth randomization or manual tuning.
A dual-agent setup separates lower-body stabilization from upper-body manipulation, enabling tasks like replacing light bulbs and handing over boxes on the ladder.

talks.title: TactileStep: Sole Tactile Learning for Regulating Foot--Terrain Interaction in Humanoid Locomotion
talks.summary: TactileStep adds sole pressure sensing to humanoid locomotion. It compresses insole readings into normal force, contact area and center of pressure, and uses phase-specific rewards that regulate touchdown, landing peaks and stance support on a Unitree G1.
takeaways: The three compact tactile features are layout-agnostic, so the same features work in simulation and on hardware.
Compared with a baseline, TactileStep lands more softly and quietly and keeps more of the sole in contact during stance, especially on stairs.
A variant trained with the same rewards but no tactile input lost much of the benefit, so the sensing itself matters.

talks.title: OpenHLM: An Empirical Recipe for Whole-Body Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
talks.summary: OpenHLM is an empirical study of what makes a whole-body humanoid VLA work. It covers teleoperation interface, VLA design and cheaper data sources, using a high-level policy initialized from pi-0 and the SONIC low-level tracker.
takeaways: Whole-body teleoperation enables foot use, and joint-space retargeting reached 88% average task progress versus 75% for SMPL-based targets.
Using relative action targets and dropping body-state perception together caused catastrophic failure.

Adding stationary teleop and human (UMI-style) data raised progress on new objects and instructions from 36% to 84%, and the full recipe reached 87.5% on a long-horizon fruit task with less than half the demonstration time.

talks.title: Learning Loco-Manipulation From SMPC Demonstrations With Sparse Offline-to-Online RL
talks.summary: The authors scale GPU sampling-based MPC in simulation into a large offline dataset of loco-manipulation demonstrations. They then train with sparse rewards using offline-to-online RL (FastTD3), avoiding manual dense reward shaping.
takeaways: Sampling-based MPC needs no training and can be iterated to a good behavior within minutes in simulation, making it a cheap expert.
Policies trained purely with sparse rewards transferred zero-shot to Spot with an arm, including pushing boxes and rolling tires.
The same pipeline also worked on a Unitree G1, showing cross-embodiment applicability.

talks.title: CMP: Robust Whole-Body Tracking for Loco-Manipulation via Competence Manifold Projection
talks.summary: Competence Manifold Projection makes whole-body trackers robust to infeasible or out-of-distribution commands by projecting them onto actions the policy truly masters. It reduces the MDP to a single-step safety test, uses a GAE-style competence estimate, and corrects in an isomorphic latent space with a single norm check.
takeaways: Instead of failing catastrophically, the robot does its best, for example turning a step-up into a step-forward when no box exists or squatting when told to sit without a chair.
Real-world survival under OOD commands rose from 0% to 87% with negligible added latency or tracking error.
The safety does not cost in-distribution agility, which still covers gimbal-like end-effector holding and catching objects midair.

talks.title: ResSafe: Learning Safety Filtering with Residual Reinforcement Learning for Humanoids
talks.summary: ResSafe freezes a performance-only humanoid policy and trains a residual RL policy that adds safety corrections. The reward is simply +1 per step alive with a small penalty on the correction.
takeaways: Decoupling safety from performance gave a better trade-off than training a single policy on both objectives.
On cart-pole, the learned residual closely matched a minimal safety filter from discriminating hyperplanes, with a slightly larger margin.
On a G1 with random payloads, ResSafe fell far less often than baselines and generalized to unseen reference policies.

talks.title: Humanoid Navigation in Cluttered Environments with a Whole-Body Vision-Language-Action Model
talks.summary: The authors present a three-system whole-body VLA for humanoid navigation through cluttered indoor scenes. A navigation foundation model, a diffusion-transformer action expert with real-time chunking, and an RL low-level tracker are trained on more than 64,000 simulated trajectories with language.
takeaways: Planar 2D action spaces limit navigation among 3D obstacles, which requires coordinating arms, torso and gait.
Training data comes purely from simulation, using potential fields for upper-body avoidance and footstep retargeting for the lower body.
The model reports state-of-the-art results on 2D and 3D navigation benchmarks and runs on a real Unitree G1 with remote inference.
author_affiliations: UC Berkeley / The University of Hong Kong

talks.title: VisionSIM: Beyond Idealized Sensors — A Multi-Modal Simulator for Robot Perception
talks.summary: VisionSIM is a physically grounded multi-sensor simulator that treats sensor realism as a first-class concern. It models cameras, event, SPAD, time-of-flight and thermal sensors with raw measurements and configurable parameters.
takeaways: Existing simulators either cover few modalities with high fidelity or many modalities with idealized models, and VisionSIM aims to push this trade-off frontier.
Failure modes like ambient-light corruption, blur, ToF phase wrapping and history-dependent thermal effects emerge naturally from the sensor physics.
The authors release a large synchronized multimodal indoor dataset with ground-truth annotations.

talks.title: MosaicIMU: Composing Carrier Experts for Generalizable Neural Inertial Odometry
talks.summary: MosaicIMU is a carrier-conditioned mixture-of-experts for neural inertial odometry across heterogeneous platforms. It fuses predicted velocities with a history-aware EKF and offers two adaptation modes: a lightweight residual branch for offline adaptation and router-based sample selection for online adaptation.
takeaways: Fixed per-carrier heads treat carrier identity rigidly, while composing expert features per sample transfers better.
Pretrained MosaicIMU reduced average ATE and RTE by 40% and 34% across carriers.
In online adaptation on a campus vehicle running on a Jetson Orin, trajectory error fell from 42.60 m to 7.60 m.
author_affiliations: Beijing Information Science and Technology University

talks.title: Anchor3R: Streaming 3D Reconstruction with Transient Anchors for Long-Horizon Visual Mapping
talks.affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences / University of Chinese Academy of Sciences / Horizon Robotics
talks.summary: Anchor3R performs long-horizon streaming 3D reconstruction by treating the current frame as a transient anchor instead of a fixed reference. It predicts relative poses within a bounded window and combines online motion averaging with loop closure.
takeaways: Trained on only 48-frame clips, it reconstructs routes of about 12,000 images and nearly 3 km.
Rebuilding pose queries when the anchor moves stops stale coordinate assumptions from propagating and keeps training and inference consistent.
A fixed-size window keeps GPU memory bounded, with no chunk resets or cross-chunk alignment needed.

talks.title: SidewalkBench: Benchmarking Visual Navigation on Urban Sidewalks
talks.summary: SidewalkBench is a GPU-simulated benchmark for camera-only visual navigation on urban sidewalks. It combines procedural and real-scanned scenes with event-triggered pedestrian behaviors, and evaluates unit-test, pedestrian-reactive and long-horizon scenarios.
takeaways: Across nine benchmarked models, those trained on sidewalk data far outperform general navigation models, and more data helps further.
Pedestrian interaction, such as crosswalks and stop gestures, is a major weakness of nearly all models.
Even the best model averages 0.68 failures per 100 m on long-horizon routes.

talks.title: From Region Arrival to Instance-Level Grounding in Vision-and-Language Navigation
talks.summary: The authors identify a 'last-3-meter grounding gap' in vision-and-language navigation, where agents count as successful inside the radius but do not face or see the target. They propose instance-level metrics, a new dataset, and REALM, a plug-and-play refinement module.
takeaways: True success should require stopping close to, facing, and seeing the target object.
REALM uses only egocentric RGB and the instruction, with visibility-aware stopping, and grounds the target with OWLv2, needing no backbone changes.
It was demonstrated on a real robot after UniNaVid and on a Unitree G1 for navigate-and-grasp tasks.

talks.title: OSCAR: Obstacle Survival Curves for Adaptive Robot Navigation
talks.summary: OSCAR learns class-specific survival functions for how long obstacles persist on a route network. It uses them to set a patience threshold for each encounter, deciding whether to wait or reroute, with a VLM classifying each obstacle.
takeaways: Fixed rules like always-wait, always-reroute or wait-only-for-people waste time because they ignore how long obstacles actually last in a given environment.
Rerouting yields right-censored observations, which survival models handle naturally.
In simulation OSCAR improves with experience, approaches an oracle with ground-truth survival functions, and beats the heuristic baselines.

talks.title: TRIAD Planner : Three-Level Robust Imitation Learning for Autonomous Driving
talks.summary: TRIAD addresses distribution shift in Transformer driving planners at three levels: it constrains excessive ego-state attention, adds offline VLM-derived agent-priority guidance, and uses CVaR-based tail-risk weighting during trajectory selection.
takeaways: Imitation-learned planners can shortcut on ego-state features, for example accelerating when the expert stopped for a pedestrian.
VLM priority weights used only at training time steer attention toward relevant agents such as crossing pedestrians.
Closed-loop nuPlan performance improves with no added inference time.

talks.title: Collaborative Planning for UAV-UGV Teams under Operational Constraints via Masked Error-bounded Neuro-Symbolic Diffusion
talks.summary: The authors plan joint actions for UAV-UGV teams, with UGVs serving as mobile recharging stations, using a masked neuro-symbolic diffusion model. Logic-induced admissibility enforces energy, traversability and recharging constraints during sampling.
takeaways: First-order logic rules over a heterogeneous graph context make hard operational constraints enforceable inside diffusion sampling.
Error-bounded inference scheduling picks the next position to unmask by minimizing predictive entropy, which improves plan optimality.
The approach was validated in a ROS city simulation and in a mixed-reality setup with Crazyflie UAVs and LIMO UGVs.

talks.title: SCoCaT: Success Conditioned Constrained Reinforcement Learning for Spacecraft Docking
talks.summary: SCoCaT fixes a failure mode of termination-based constrained RL (CaT) in goal-reaching tasks such as spacecraft docking, where agents hover near the goal to avoid violations. It adds a success critic whose return bootstraps over early terminations.
takeaways: The authors derive a factor kappa that explains how stochastic terminations shrink the value near the goal and cause the hovering behavior.
Summing advantages from the success critic and the damped CaT stream within PPO restores goal reaching without constraint violations.
The method gave a 250-fold increase in task completion on a floating platform and transferred zero-shot to a real thruster-equipped testbed.

talks.title: Atlas: A Unified World Model for Generation and Reconstruction
talks.summary: After an introduction by her former PhD student Yuke Zhu, Fei-Fei Li argues that robotics' core needs (representing the world, predicting the consequences of actions, and simulating data) map onto world-modeling problems. She presents Atlas from World Labs, a multimodal autoregressive diffusion transformer trained from scratch that takes text, images, video, depth or gray-box inputs and outputs camera-conditioned frames. Atlas spans dense reconstruction, sparse reconstruction from a few views, and pure generation in one model, illustrated by reconstructing Stanford's Main Quad from 2, 8 and 33 ground-level photos. She shows strong third-party camera-control generation results, depth and Gaussian-splat reconstruction results, a real-time 15 fps distilled version, and early robot sim-to-real uses. A planned premiere of a promotional video failed because of AV problems, causing a long pause near the end.
takeaways: Li describes Atlas's core idea as 'viewpoint is all you need': predicting the next viewpoint with strong camera conditioning, analogous to next-token prediction.
One model covers the full range from dense reconstruction through sparse reconstruction to text-only generation.
On a third-party benchmark with about half a million human judgments, Atlas ranked first for camera-controlled generation by a clear margin.
Atlas beat specialized models on depth prediction across seven datasets and was competitive on Gaussian-splat reconstruction error.
A distilled real-time version runs at 15 fps, and World Labs is testing Atlas worlds for training navigation and manipulation robots with zero-shot real deployment.

talks.title: Fireside Chat: Fei-Fei Li & Lisa Su
talks.summary: Peter Stone moderates a conversation between Lisa Su (AMD chair and CEO) and Fei-Fei Li, framed around AMD's in-process acquisition of World Labs and Li's upcoming role as AMD chief scientist. Su describes physical AI and robotics as an opportunity worth hundreds of billions of dollars that needs hardware-software co-design and compute at every scale, from cloud to edge. Li argues that AI is computing and calls failing to resource the public sector one of the biggest misses of this moment, and Su commits AMD to dedicating compute to academic research. Answering audience questions, they discuss whether AMD will have a robotics team, whether a PhD is still worthwhile, energy-efficient AI versus the brain's 20 watts, and advice for students.
takeaways: Su expects no single model to win across applications: frontier LLMs will be complemented by specialized models that are cheaper, more power-efficient and lower-latency.
Li believes robotics will push compute to its next level, both for training and at the edge.
Li calls for public-sector compute (citing the NAIRR effort) as essential for blue-sky research, workforce training and independent evaluation of AI.
Su says AMD already has a robotics and physical-AI research effort and plans to invest significantly more under Li.
Both describe a PhD as worth it for those driven by curiosity, and Li notes that the brain's efficiency reflects billions of years of evolution, which should not be confused with training cost.
Their parting advice was to hold onto timeless values like curiosity, integrity and fearlessness (Li) and to run toward the hardest problems (Su).

talks.title: Debate: "The current recipe of behavior cloning pre-training and in-domain fine-tuning will lead to commercially viable generalist robots"
talks.summary: Vincent Vanhoucke moderates a formal debate on the motion that the current recipe of behavior-cloning pre-training plus in-domain fine-tuning will lead to commercially viable generalist robots. He defines 'generalist' as zero-shot retaskable by an end user within a well-specified domain, and 'commercially viable' as profitable on customer revenue. Chelsea Finn, Pulkit Agrawal and Marc Toussaint argue for the motion, citing large in-domain data, optimizing for reliability, and narrow but lucrative domains like pick-and-place. Leslie Kaelbling, Edward Johns and Yonatan Bisk argue against it, pointing to the cost of covering the state space with human demonstrations, heterogeneous architectures, and the need for reasoning beyond imitation. Polls of the audience before and after the debate showed the room leaning con, with little change in opinion.
takeaways: Finn argues that reliability is the key to commercial value and that it comes from large in-domain data plus post-training optimized for success, which is how LLMs became useful.

Kaelbling argues that BC has not shown 'explosive generalization' because physical tasks, unlike language, were not designed to be learnable, and that learned models are more disentangleable than policies.
Johns argues that paying people to collect task-specific data is uneconomical for most tasks (laundry folding is the exception) and points to simulation as a likely route.
Agrawal argues that system-2 planning is largely solved by LLMs, the bottleneck is system-1 contact-rich control, and the right metric is throughput (speed times reliability), not accuracy.

Toussaint argues that narrow commercial domains can be covered by data even if this is not the best science, while Bisk argues that imitation alone cannot produce the reasoning about the unseen that safety-critical deployment needs.
Much of the debate turned on definitions, such as whether simulation and RL fine-tuning count as part of 'the current recipe'.

talks.title: Musical Interlude: Robot-Conducted String Quartet
talks.summary: General chair Peter Stone plays violin in a string quartet with cellist Shu Scott, violist Alan Chen and violinist Mary Brown, all with UT Austin ties. They perform the last movement of Dvořák's 'American' String Quartet and 'Spider Dreams' by the Turtle Island String Quartet. A robot was supposed to conduct, but it did not come out because of a technical failure. Yuke Zhu then thanks Stone and previews the awards.
takeaways: The planned robot conductor did not appear because of a technical failure, which Stone joked was another AV failure of the day.
The interlude was framed as showing that top researchers can also excel at other pursuits.
The interlude led directly into the closing ceremony and best paper awards.

talks.title: Closing Remarks, Awards & Farewell
talks.summary: General chair Yuke Zhu thanks the organizing committee, reviewers, the Robot Learning Foundation, about 75 volunteers and the sponsors, noting the conference roughly tripled in size this year. Awards committee chair Katerina Fragkiadaki explains that the committee read all 21 oral papers, picked six finalists (SuperMimic, Play2Perfect, GRAIL, RoboTTT, What Are We Actually Benchmarking in Robot Manipulation?, and the distilled tree search rearrangement paper), and chose two winners. The Best Student Paper Award went to RoboTTT and the Best Conference Paper Award went to SuperMimic. Vincent Vanhoucke announces a year-round Transactions on Robot Learning and a Test of Time award starting next year, and Ken Goldberg reflects on a 'revenue crisis' in robotics and announces CoRL 2027 in Paris.
takeaways: Best Student Paper Award: RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies.
Best Conference Paper Award: SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model.
Awards were judged on significance and long-term impact, originality, technical soundness, clarity, and reproducibility and openness.
A new Transactions on Robot Learning accepts submissions year-round, with top papers presented at CoRL, and a Test of Time award for papers from 2017 onward starts next year.
Goldberg argues the field must now deliver reliability, throughput and interpretability to earn revenue, and announces CoRL 2027 in Paris.
